explanation: The clinical definition of AIDS includes a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/uL or the development of specific opportunistic conditions regardless of the count. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h1)

question: Which body fluid carries the highest concentration of the virus capable of horizontal transmission?

options.A: Seminal and vaginal fluids
options.B: Unbroken tear secretions
options.C: Saliva in small quantities
options.D: Perspiration and sweat

explanation: Genital secretions and blood contain high viral titers necessary for transmission, unlike casual contact fluids such as sweat or tears. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h2)

question: What describes vertical transmission of the virus?

options.A: Transmission through accidental needle stick injuries in a clinical laboratory setting
options.B: Infection acquired via sharing contaminated drinking vessels in a household
options.C: Spread through airborne droplets generated by coughing or sneezing in closed spaces
options.D: Spread from an infected mother to her child during pregnancy, birth, or breastfeeding

explanation: Vertical transmission specifically refers to the passing of pathogens from parent to child during the perinatal period. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h2)

question: What is another common clinical term used for the clinical latency stage of the disease?

options.A: Acute retroviral syndrome
options.B: Terminal immunological collapse
options.C: Chronic HIV infection
options.D: Window period phase

explanation: During clinical latency, the virus is still active but replicates at low levels, which is why it is also referred to as chronic HIV infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h3)

question: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of the acute infection stage following initial exposure?

options.A: Permanent stabilization of CD4 counts above normal levels
options.B: Flu-like symptoms accompanied by a high viral load
options.C: Total absence of any circulating virus in the bloodstream
options.D: Immediate onset of severe opportunistic malignancies

explanation: Acute infection often mimics mononucleosis or influenza, featuring fever, fatigue, and swollen lymph nodes alongside massive viral replication. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h3)

question: Which fungal infection frequently presents as white plaques on the oral mucous membranes of immunocompromised individuals?

options.A: Pneumocystis pneumonia
options.B: Oral candidiasis
options.C: Cryptococcal meningitis
options.D: Kaposi sarcoma

explanation: Oral candidiasis, or thrush, is an opportunistic fungal infection that readily overgrows when cellular immunity is depressed. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h4)

question: Why are opportunistic infections dangerous to individuals with advanced immunodeficiency?

options.A: The weakened immune system cannot defend against organisms that are normally harmless to healthy people
options.B: Normal flora inside the human body turns into malignant cancer cells within hours
options.C: The opportunistic organisms produce toxins that immediately destroy all internal organs
options.D: These specific pathogens mutate rapidly to become completely resistant to all known antibiotics

explanation: Opportunistic infections take advantage of a failing immune system, causing severe disease from pathogens that a robust immune system easily controls. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of a viral load test in clinical management?

options.A: To measure the exact amount of active virus circulating in the blood
options.B: To evaluate liver enzyme function before starting medication
options.C: To determine the absolute number of healthy red blood cells
options.D: To screen for the presence of bacterial pneumonia pathogens

explanation: Viral load quantification measures copies of viral RNA per milliliter, guiding clinicians on whether treatment is successfully suppressing replication. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h5)

question: What makes fourth-generation screening assays superior to older antibody-only tests?

options.A: They detect the p24 antigen alongside antibodies, reducing the window period before detection
options.B: They can identify the exact strain of the virus infecting the patient instantly
options.C: They completely eliminate the need for any confirmatory laboratory blood draws
options.D: They rely exclusively on urine samples rather than invasive venipuncture

explanation: By identifying the p24 viral protein before the body generates detectable antibodies, fourth-generation tests catch infections much earlier. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h5)

question: What is the main goal of consistent antiretroviral therapy for an infected individual?

options.A: Completely eradicating all dormant virus from animal reservoirs
options.B: Achieving and maintaining an undetectable viral load
options.C: Permanently curing the underlying genetic mutation
options.D: Preventing the normal production of white blood cells

explanation: While therapy does not cure the infection, it suppresses viral replication to undetectable levels, preserving immune function and preventing transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h6)

question: Why is strict adherence to a daily antiretroviral schedule essential for patients?

options.A: Missing a single dose causes immediate and total permanent blindness
options.B: The medications decompose rapidly in the stomach if taken at irregular hours
options.C: Irregular dosing triggers severe allergic reactions in all patient populations
options.D: Inconsistent medication intake promotes the development of drug-resistant viral strains

explanation: Sub-therapeutic drug levels in the blood allow replicating viruses to mutate and develop resistance to the prescribed medications. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h6)

question: What describes the function of Pre-exposure Prophylaxis?

options.A: Administering a therapeutic vaccine to individuals who already have full-blown AIDS
options.B: Taking antiretroviral medications daily by HIV-negative individuals to prevent infection
options.C: Providing emergency antibiotics to treat acute opportunistic pneumonia infections
options.D: Using topical barrier creams to eliminate bacteria during sexual intercourse

explanation: PrEP is a biomedical prevention strategy where individuals at ongoing risk take medications regularly to block potential viral acquisition. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h7)

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for a healthcare worker following an accidental needle-stick injury from an infected source?

options.A: Taking high-dose vitamins to boost general immune resistance
options.B: Initiating post-exposure prophylaxis medications as soon as possible
options.C: Discontinuing all work duties permanently without further assessment
options.D: Waiting three months before seeking any medical evaluation or blood work

explanation: PEP should be started promptly, ideally within hours of exposure, to reduce the likelihood of systemic viral establishment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T1#GNS216_U6_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary genetic material found inside the HIV virion?

options.A: Double-stranded RNA
options.B: Double-stranded DNA
options.C: Single-stranded DNA
options.D: Single-stranded RNA

explanation: HIV is a retrovirus that packages two identical copies of single-stranded RNA within its central capsid. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which viral glycoprotein is directly responsible for attaching to receptors on the surface of host immune cells?

options.A: gp120
options.B: Reverse transcriptase
options.C: Protease
options.D: Integrase

explanation: The surface glycoprotein gp120 recognizes and binds to CD4 receptors and coreceptors on target cells, initiating viral entry. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which coreceptor is primarily utilized by macrophage-tropic strains of HIV during early infection?

options.A: CD8
options.B: CXCR4
options.C: CCR5
options.D: CD4

explanation: CCR5 is the principal chemokine coreceptor used by transmitted strains of HIV to gain entry into macrophages and dendritic cells. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: A patient with a rare genetic mutation lacking functional CCR5 coreceptors is exposed to HIV. What is the most likely immunological outcome?

options.A: Severe depletion of circulating CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells
options.B: Rapid development of opportunistic fungal infections
options.C: Immediate progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
options.D: High resistance to infection by most strains of the virus

explanation: Without the CCR5 coreceptor, the virus cannot easily attach and fuse with the host cell, conferring strong natural resistance against infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h2)

question: Which viral enzyme is responsible for inserting transcribed viral DNA into the host cell genome?

options.A: Protease
options.B: Reverse transcriptase
options.C: DNA polymerase
options.D: Integrase

explanation: Integrase is the specialized enzyme that facilitates the incorporation of viral DNA into host chromosomes. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: Why does reverse transcriptase frequently contribute to the high genetic variability of HIV?

options.A: It converts host cellular proteins directly into viral structural components
options.B: It lacks a proofreading mechanism, leading to a high mutation rate
options.C: It rapidly replicates without utilizing any cellular resources
options.D: It actively destroys host DNA to make room for viral particles

explanation: Because reverse transcriptase makes frequent transcription errors without proofreading, mutations accumulate rapidly, resulting in diverse viral variants. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the hallmark clinical feature of the acute phase of HIV infection?

options.A: Permanent restoration of CD4+ cell counts
options.B: Complete absence of viral particles in blood
options.C: Instantaneous development of Kaposi sarcoma
options.D: Flu-like symptoms and high viral load

explanation: Acute infection features a massive viral surge that often triggers a self-limiting acute retroviral syndrome resembling severe influenza. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: During which natural stage of HIV infection is a patient most likely to remain completely asymptomatic for years while experiencing a steady decline in immune function?

options.A: Primary seroconversion
options.B: Clinical latency
options.C: Advanced AIDS
options.D: Acute retroviral syndrome

explanation: During the clinical latency period, the virus remains active at lower levels, but the patient typically experiences few or no symptoms for an extended duration. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h4)

question: Which WHO clinical stage of HIV infection includes pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Stage 3
options.B: Stage 1
options.C: Stage 2
options.D: Stage 4

explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis and severe, unexplained weight loss are classified under WHO clinical stage 3. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: A patient presents with persistent generalized lymphadenopathy and no other systemic complaints. According to the WHO staging system, what is the correct classification?

options.A: Clinical Stage 4
options.B: Clinical Stage 2
options.C: Clinical Stage 1
options.D: Clinical Stage 3

explanation: Persistent generalized lymphadenopathy combined with an asymptomatic state falls under WHO Clinical Stage 1. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h5)

question: What is the specific CD4+ T-cell count threshold that defines the progression from HIV to AIDS in the absence of defining illnesses?

options.A: Below 50 cells/mm³
options.B: Below 200 cells/mm³
options.C: Below 500 cells/mm³
options.D: Below 1000 cells/mm³

explanation: A CD4+ cell count dropping below 200 cells per cubic millimeter is a definitive clinical criterion for the diagnosis of AIDS. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary consequence of chronic immune activation during progressive HIV infection?

options.A: Enhancement of CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell longevity
options.B: Exhaustion and structural damage to lymphoid tissues
options.C: Immediate regeneration of damaged mucosal barriers
options.D: Permanent eradication of viral reservoirs in the body

explanation: Persistent immune activation forces continuous lymphocyte turnover, eventually causing immune exhaustion and destruction of the architectural framework of lymphoid organs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which malignancy is strongly associated with advanced HIV/AIDS and caused by human herpesvirus 8?

options.A: Kaposi sarcoma
options.B: Multiple myeloma
options.C: Chronic myeloid leukemia
options.D: Cervical carcinoma

explanation: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor driven by human herpesvirus 8 infection that frequently manifests in severely immunocompromised HIV patients. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)

question: Why are opportunistic infections able to cause severe, life-threatening illness exclusively in individuals with advanced HIV?

options.A: These specific pathogens only replicate in the presence of antiretroviral drugs
options.B: Bacteria and fungi mutate rapidly once they enter the human bloodstream
options.C: The pathogens directly stimulate massive overproduction of healthy red blood cells
options.D: The loss of cell-mediated immunity prevents adequate defense against low-virulence organisms

explanation: Opportunistic pathogens are typically controlled by a functioning immune system, but severe CD4+ depletion leaves the body defenseless against them. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T2#GNS216_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary cellular receptor targeted by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus during infection?

options.A: Beta-2 microglobulin
options.B: CD8 receptors
options.C: Immunoglobulin M
options.D: CD4 receptors

explanation: HIV specifically targets and binds to CD4 receptors found primarily on helper T-lymphocytes, leading to their eventual destruction. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h1)

question: Why is reverse transcriptase a critical enzyme for the Human Immunodeficiency Virus life cycle?

options.A: It cleaves precursor proteins during viral maturation
options.B: It fuses the viral envelope with the host membrane
options.C: It converts viral RNA into double-stranded DNA
options.D: It integrates viral DNA into the host genome

explanation: Reverse transcriptase allows the single-stranded RNA genetic material of the virus to be transcribed into a DNA format that the host cell can process. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h1)

question: What clinical threshold defines the transition from chronic HIV infection to AIDS based on immunological parameters?

options.A: CD4 count below 500 cells/mm3
options.B: Viral load dropping to zero copies/mL
options.C: Total lymphocyte count above 4000 cells/mm3
options.D: CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3

explanation: A CD4+ T-lymphocyte count dropping below 200 cells/mm³ is a standard diagnostic criterion for defining AIDS, indicating profound immunosuppression. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h2)

question: A patient presents with a fever, generalized rash, and sore throat occurring two weeks after potential exposure to HIV. This presentation is most characteristic of which stage?

options.A: Acute HIV infection
options.B: Advanced AIDS dementia
options.C: Asymptomatic carrier state
options.D: Clinical latency stage

explanation: The initial weeks following infection often present with acute retroviral syndrome symptoms resembling infectious mononucleosis. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h2)

question: Which fungal pathogen is the most frequent cause of interstitial pneumonia in patients with advanced AIDS?

options.A: Pneumocystis jirovecii
options.B: Cryptococcus neoformans
options.C: Candida albicans
options.D: Aspergillus fumigatus

explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is a hallmark opportunistic infection seen when CD4 counts drop significantly. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h3)

question: Which of the following conditions is NOT a classic opportunistic infection or malignancy associated with advanced AIDS?

options.A: Cryptococcal meningitis
options.B: Kaposi sarcoma
options.C: Oral candidiasis
options.D: Pernicious anemia

explanation: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune condition affecting vitamin B12 absorption, not an opportunistic infection or AIDS-defining malignancy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h3)

question: What viral component is detected alongside antibodies in fourth-generation HIV screening assays to shorten the window period?

options.A: Integrase enzyme
options.B: gp120 envelope glycoprotein
options.C: Reverse transcriptase enzyme
options.D: p24 capsid antigen

explanation: Fourth-generation tests detect the p24 antigen, which appears in the blood earlier than antibodies during acute infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h4)

question: Why is a nucleic acid test particularly valuable during the acute phase of an HIV infection?

options.A: It measures the absolute CD4 lymphocyte count in the blood
options.B: It directly detects circulating viral RNA before antibodies develop
options.C: It confirms the presence of opportunistic fungal infections
options.D: It evaluates liver enzyme function prior to starting therapy

explanation: NAT assays measure viral RNA directly, making them effective for diagnosing infection during the early window period before the body mounts an antibody response. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h4)

question: What does a plasma viral load test measure in the management of an infected patient?

options.A: The total white blood cell count minus neutrophils
options.B: The volume of antibodies produced against the p24 antigen
options.C: The percentage of functional CD4+ T-lymphocytes remaining
options.D: The concentration of viral RNA copies per milliliter of blood

explanation: Viral load quantification measures the actual amount of circulating viral RNA, indicating the speed of viral replication and treatment success. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h5)

question: How does an undetectable viral load result impact clinical decision-making and patient counseling?

options.A: It means the CD4 count has returned to normal without medication
options.B: It signals that opportunistic infection prophylaxis can be doubled
options.C: It proves the patient has completely cleared the virus from their body
options.D: It indicates effective viral suppression from antiretroviral therapy

explanation: An undetectable viral load means the medication is working well to suppress replication, though the virus remains latent within reservoirs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h5)

question: What constellation of constitutional symptoms is commonly referred to as HIV wasting syndrome during clinical evaluation?

options.A: Jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, pruritus, and dark urine
options.B: Severe headache, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and confusion
options.C: Hypertension, peripheral edema, shortness of breath, and fatigue
options.D: Fever, chronic diarrhea, night sweats, and significant weight loss

explanation: HIV wasting syndrome is characterized by involuntary weight loss greater than ten percent of baseline body weight, accompanied by chronic diarrhea or weakness and fever. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h6)

question: A nurse is performing an initial physical assessment on a newly diagnosed patient. Which finding requires immediate further investigation for an opportunistic infection?

options.A: Healed scars from a childhood varicella infection
options.B: White plaques on the buccal mucosa that scrape off
options.C: Mild localized erythema around a recent venipuncture site
options.D: Asymptomatic baseline seasonal allergic rhinitis

explanation: Oral candidiasis (thrush) indicated by scrapable white plaques suggests underlying immunosuppression requiring prompt antifungal therapy evaluation. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T3#GNS216_U6_T3_h6)

question: What is the primary biological goal of antiretroviral therapy in HIV management?

options.A: Complete eradication of the viral reservoir from the body
options.B: Permanent stimulation of bone marrow cell production
options.C: Neutralization of circulating antibodies in the blood
options.D: Suppression of viral replication to undetectable levels

explanation: Current antiretroviral drugs cannot completely eradicate latent viral reservoirs, so the realistic primary goal is maximum and sustained suppression of viral replication. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h1)

question: How does achieving sustained viral suppression directly benefit a patient's immune system?

options.A: It triggers immediate destruction of all dormant viral particles.
options.B: It allows the CD4 cell count to gradually recover and increase.
options.C: It eliminates the need for baseline kidney function testing.
options.D: It permanently repairs damaged lymph node architecture.

explanation: When active viral replication is halted, the ongoing destruction of helper T-cells stops, enabling the immune system to rebuild its CD4 counts over time. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h1)

question: Which drug class prevents viral DNA from being inserted into the host cell chromosome?

options.A: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors
options.B: Protease inhibitors
options.C: Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors
options.D: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors

explanation: Integrase inhibitors specifically block the enzyme integrase, which is responsible for splicing the genetic material of HIV into the host cell's own DNA. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h2)

question: Why is combination therapy using multiple drug classes standard practice for HIV treatment?

options.A: It bypasses the need for routine laboratory viral load testing.
options.B: It forces the virus to mutate faster into milder strains.
options.C: It interrupts several distinct stages of the viral life cycle simultaneously.
options.D: It completely prevents any potential adverse metabolic side effects.

explanation: Attacking the virus at multiple different steps of its replication cycle overwhelms its mutation capacity and prevents rapid drug resistance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h2)

question: What is the preferred anchor drug in current standard first-line ART regimens in Nigeria?

options.A: Lopinavir
options.B: Nevirapine
options.C: Dolutegravir
options.D: Efavirenz

explanation: Dolutegravir is an integrase inhibitor that is currently favored in national guidelines due to its high efficacy, rapid viral suppression, and high barrier to drug resistance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h3)

question: A patient on a first-line TDF/3TC/DTG regimen experiences confirmed treatment failure due to viral rebound. What class of drug is typically introduced in the second-line regimen?

options.A: Boosted protease inhibitors
options.B: CCR5 co-receptor antagonists
options.C: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors
options.D: Unboosted integrase strand transfer inhibitors

explanation: Second-line regimens typically switch the primary drug class to a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor combined with a fresh NRTI backbone after first-line failure. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h3)

question: Which baseline laboratory test is specifically required before prescribing a Tenofovir-containing regimen to protect patient safety?

options.A: Thyroid stimulating hormone
options.B: Renal function tests
options.C: Serum lipid profile
options.D: Fast blood glucose

explanation: Tenofovir can cause nephrotoxicity, making baseline and ongoing assessment of kidney function via serum creatinine and calculated clearance critical. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h4)

question: What is the clinical purpose of performing a baseline CD4 cell count prior to starting ART?

options.A: To confirm the specific viral subtype infecting the patient
options.B: To evaluate the current degree of immune system compromise
options.C: To determine the precise dosing schedule of protease inhibitors
options.D: To measure the metabolic clearance rate of the drugs

explanation: The CD4 count measures helper T-lymphocyte levels, revealing how severely the immune system has been damaged and indicating risks for specific opportunistic infections. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h4)

question: What threshold of plasma viral load generally defines clinical treatment failure requiring intensive adherence counseling or regimen switch?

options.A: Above 10,000 copies/mL
options.B: Above 50 copies/mL
options.C: Above 500 copies/mL
options.D: Above 1,000 copies/mL

explanation: National and international guidelines define virological failure as a viral load persistently above 1,000 copies/mL after at least six months of continuous therapy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h5)

question: A patient newly started on a regimen containing efavirenz reports vivid dreams and mild dizziness. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Reassure the patient that these central nervous system symptoms often subside within a few weeks.
options.B: Immediately stop all antiretroviral medications permanently.
options.C: Switch the patient immediately to a second-line protease inhibitor regimen.
options.D: Double the dose of the medication to accelerate drug tolerance.

explanation: Central nervous system side effects from efavirenz are common during the first few weeks of therapy and typically resolve on their own without requiring drug discontinuation. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h5)

question: Why is concurrent administration of rifampicin for tuberculosis and certain antiretroviral drugs clinically challenging?

options.A: Antiretroviral drugs completely neutralize the bactericidal action of rifampicin.
options.B: Rifampicin alters liver enzymes and can lower antiretroviral blood concentrations.
options.C: The combination causes immediate, irreversible renal failure.
options.D: Rifampicin drastically increases bone marrow suppression.

explanation: Rifampicin is a potent hepatic enzyme inducer that accelerates the metabolism of various antiretrovirals, potentially reducing them to sub-therapeutic levels. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h6)

question: A patient taking a protease inhibitor complains of persistent nausea after morning doses. What simple management strategy can a nurse suggest?

options.A: Skip the morning dose and take a double dose in the evening.
options.B: Crush the tablets to speed up gastric emptying.
options.C: Take the medication with food to decrease gastrointestinal irritation.
options.D: Stop the medication for one week until nausea resolves.

explanation: Many antiretroviral medications can be taken with food to alleviate mild gastrointestinal upset, improving overall patient comfort and adherence. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h6)

question: What is the approximate minimum level of medication adherence generally required to maintain viral suppression and prevent resistance?

options.A: At least 85%
options.B: At least 50%
options.C: At least 95%
options.D: At least 70%

explanation: Antiretroviral therapy requires near-perfect adherence—typically defined as taking at least 95% of doses on schedule—to prevent the virus from mutating and developing resistance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary danger of chronic, low-level non-adherence to antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Permanent physical tolerance to all drug classes
options.B: Complete elimination of latent viral reservoirs
options.C: Development of drug-resistant viral mutations
options.D: Rapid healing of damaged CD4 receptors

explanation: Incomplete adherence creates low drug concentrations in the blood that fail to suppress replication, giving the virus an opportunity to mutate and evade the drugs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T4#GNS216_U6_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary effect of chronic HIV infection on a person's basal metabolic rate?

options.A: It causes the metabolic rate to fluctuate wildly
options.B: It significantly increases the metabolic rate
options.C: It has no measurable effect on metabolism
options.D: It decreases the overall metabolic rate

explanation: Fighting a chronic infection like HIV requires extra energy, which drives up the basal metabolic rate and increases daily caloric needs. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h1)

question: Why is integrating nutritional care into routine HIV clinics especially vital in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Nutritional supplements replace the need for laboratory monitoring
options.B: Baseline malnutrition can accelerate disease progression before treatment starts
options.C: Antiretroviral drugs are completely ineffective without high-protein diets
options.D: Patients in these areas refuse to take medications without food provisions

explanation: Pre-existing nutritional deficits weaken the immune system further, speeding up disease advancement before antiretroviral therapy can stabilize the patient. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h1)

question: Which macronutrient acts primarily to spare body proteins from being broken down for energy?

options.A: Fat-soluble enzymes
options.B: Trace minerals
options.C: Vitamins
options.D: Carbohydrates

explanation: Carbohydrates serve as the body's primary energy source, preventing proteins from being diverted away from their essential tissue-building functions. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h2)

question: What is the primary role of micronutrients such as zinc, selenium, and vitamins A and C in individuals living with HIV?

options.A: Directly eliminating the human immunodeficiency virus
options.B: Acting as antioxidants and supporting immune cell function
options.C: Lowering the baseline metabolic rate to prevent weight loss
options.D: Replacing the pharmacological action of antiretroviral drugs

explanation: Vitamins and minerals play vital enzymatic and antioxidant roles that protect cells from oxidative stress and bolster immune defenses. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h2)

question: What does a Mid-Upper Arm Circumference measurement primarily assess in clinical practice?

options.A: Circulating viral load and CD4 cell counts
options.B: Basal metabolic rate and energy expenditure
options.C: Total body fat percentage and hydration status
options.D: Acute malnutrition and muscle wasting

explanation: MUAC is a quick, practical anthropometric tool used to screen for acute malnutrition and loss of muscle mass, especially when weighing is difficult. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h3)

question: A patient with HIV presents to the clinic with an unintentional 10 percent weight loss over the past two months. What clinical interpretation should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: This is a normal physiological adaptation to starting new antiretroviral regimens
options.B: This suggests the patient has increased their physical activity too rapidly
options.C: This indicates potential disease progression or treatment failure requiring immediate evaluation
options.D: This confirms that micronutrient supplements are no longer necessary

explanation: Significant unintentional weight loss over a short timeframe is a red flag signaling possible opportunistic illness or failing therapy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h3)

question: Which dietary modification is most appropriate for a patient experiencing severe oral thrush and painful swallowing?

options.A: Soft, bland, and lukewarm or cool foods
options.B: Very hot liquids to sterilize the oral cavity
options.C: Dry, rough foods to scrape away lesions
options.D: Highly spiced dishes to stimulate appetite

explanation: Soft and cool foods minimize irritation to painful, inflamed oral and esophageal mucosa, making eating more manageable. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h4)

question: What is a primary long-term metabolic complication associated with certain antiretroviral medications?

options.A: Rapid regeneration of lost skeletal muscle tissue
options.B: Permanent loss of the sense of taste
options.C: Lipodystrophy and dyslipidemia
options.D: Complete cessation of pancreatic enzyme production

explanation: Long-term antiretroviral therapy can alter fat distribution and lipid profiles, raising concerns for metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h4)

question: Why are certain antiretroviral drugs prescribed to be taken on an empty stomach?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing weight gain
options.B: To prevent food from interfering with absorption or increasing side effects
options.C: To speed up the renal excretion of inactive drug metabolites
options.D: To ensure that liver enzymes remain completely inactive during digestion

explanation: Food can bind to certain medications or alter stomach acidity, reducing their uptake or worsening adverse neurological and gastrointestinal effects. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h5)

question: A patient taking efavirenz complains of severe dizziness and sleep disturbances. What nursing intervention addresses this drug-nutrient or administration issue?

options.A: Advise taking the medication on an empty stomach right before bedtime
options.B: Suggest stopping the drug until the neurological symptoms completely disappear
options.C: Recommend switching the medication to early morning with breakfast
options.D: Instruct the patient to consume a heavy fatty meal immediately before the dose

explanation: Taking efavirenz on an empty stomach at night helps the patient sleep through the peak central nervous system side effects. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h5)

question: Which practice is essential for preventing waterborne infections in immunocompromised patients?

options.A: Storing water in open clay pots to aerate it
options.B: Boiling or properly filtering all drinking water
options.C: Adding synthetic food coloring to detect impurities
options.D: Drinking rainwater directly from rooftop catchment systems

explanation: Immunocompromised individuals lack the immune reserve to fight off waterborne parasites and bacteria, making boiling or filtration mandatory. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended food safety practice for individuals with HIV?

options.A: Refrigerating cooked leftovers promptly after meals
options.B: Thoroughly washing raw fruits and vegetables before preparation
options.C: Consuming raw or undercooked eggs and meats for extra protein
options.D: Ensuring poultry reaches safe internal cooking temperatures

explanation: Raw or undercooked animal products frequently harbor dangerous bacteria like Salmonella, posing severe health risks to people with weakened immune systems. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h6)

question: What is the most effective approach when providing nutritional counseling to an economically disadvantaged patient with HIV?

options.A: Focus exclusively on medication adherence while ignoring diet
options.B: Advise the patient to fast intermittently until financial status improves
options.C: Insist on a strict imported supplement regimen to guarantee recovery
options.D: Recommend affordable, locally available food items that fit household resources

explanation: Practical dietary advice must respect the patient's financial situation by emphasizing nutritious, accessible local foods. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h7)

question: Why is involving family members in nutritional counseling sessions beneficial?

options.A: It replaces the need for professional nursing assessments
options.B: It ensures that the patient eats in total isolation
options.C: It legally obligates family members to pay for clinic medications
options.D: It improves household support for meal preparation and dietary adherence

explanation: Family involvement fosters a supportive home environment, making it easier for the patient to prepare and maintain recommended dietary changes. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T5#GNS216_U6_T5_h7)

question: What primary benefit does family support provide for a patient managing a chronic condition like HIV?

options.A: Permanent immunity against opportunistic pathogens
options.B: Enhanced retention in care and viral suppression
options.C: Immediate cure of the underlying viral infection
options.D: Complete elimination of the need for clinical check-ups

explanation: Active family involvement creates a support system that helps patients keep clinic appointments and take medications consistently, leading to better viral control. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h1)

question: Why is a family-centered care model particularly vital in resource-limited settings?

options.A: Government policies legally mandate household quarantine for infected persons
options.B: Hospitals in these regions do not provide antiretroviral medications
options.C: Extended family networks often share financial pooling and physical care tasks
options.D: Biomedical interventions are completely ineffective without herbal remedies

explanation: In many regions, households rely on collective resources and shared responsibilities to navigate the challenges of chronic illness management. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h1)

question: Which emotional response is most commonly observed among primary caregivers in households affected by HIV?

options.A: Caregiver burnout and anticipatory grief
options.B: A complete absence of emotional reaction
options.C: Euphoria regarding the modern healthcare system
options.D: Indifference toward the patient's daily needs

explanation: The continuous demand of supporting a chronically ill family member while managing social fears often leads to emotional exhaustion and worry about the future. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h2)

question: How can untreated psychological distress within a household indirectly affect clinical outcomes for the patient?

options.A: By forcing the local clinic to discharge the patient permanently
options.B: By causing a sudden biochemical mutation of the virus within the bloodstream
options.C: By physically destroying antiretroviral drug supplies stored in the home
options.D: By creating a tense environment that hinders consistent medication habits and care retention

explanation: High stress and emotional turmoil in the home disrupt daily routines, making it harder for the patient to stay engaged with treatment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h2)

question: Which strategy represents a practical way for a household member to support antiretroviral adherence?

options.A: Altering the prescribed drug dosage based on daily mood
options.B: Hiding the medication bottles to protect family privacy
options.C: Stopping treatment whenever the patient feels energetic
options.D: Linking medication administration to daily meal routines

explanation: Anchoring pill-taking to established household activities like eating meals builds a reliable daily habit. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h3)

question: A patient repeatedly forgets evening doses of antiretroviral therapy. Which family-led intervention is most appropriate to suggest?

options.A: Assigning a household member to provide gentle reminders and set phone alarms
options.B: Switching the prescription to an over-the-counter herbal alternative
options.C: Telling the patient to double the morning dose to make up for lost time
options.D: Withholding all medication until the patient remembers independently

explanation: Using external cues and family accountability directly targets forgetfulness without altering the medication regimen improperly. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h3)

question: Which household practice is scientifically unfounded and reflects persisting HIV-related stigma?

options.A: Providing a separate bedroom purely for comfort during an illness
options.B: Washing soiled clothing with standard household detergent and water
options.C: Sharing meals from the same family pot using clean serving spoons
options.D: Segregating eating utensils and sleeping quarters for the infected person

explanation: The virus is not transmitted through casual contact, sharing utensils, or sharing living spaces, making segregation unnecessary and harmful. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary consequence of experiencing stigma and discrimination from immediate family members?

options.A: The virus naturally mutates into a less responsive strain
options.B: Antiretroviral drugs become completely absorbed by the digestive system
options.C: The patient develops permanent immunity against secondary infections
options.D: Patients may hide their medication and disengage from healthcare services

explanation: Fear of judgment at home often drives individuals to conceal their status and avoid clinic visits, threatening their health. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h4)

question: Why is nutritional support emphasized as a core component of household HIV care?

options.A: It guarantees an immediate cure for opportunistic respiratory infections
options.B: It supports immune function and works synergistically with antiretroviral therapy
options.C: It completely replaces the need for daily prescription medications
options.D: It prevents any natural fluctuations in body weight over time

explanation: Proper nutrition helps the body process medications effectively, maintains strength, and keeps the immune system robust. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h5)

question: When counseling a family on dietary management in low-resource settings, what should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: Insisting on strict adherence to a single exotic grain variety
options.B: Utilizing locally available, affordable, and nutrient-dense food items
options.C: Restricting food intake to reduce the metabolic load on the liver
options.D: Importing expensive specialized dietary supplements from overseas

explanation: Sustainability is vital, so recommendations must focus on foods that families can easily access and afford within their local economy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h5)

question: What is a recommended approach for a patient who is hesitant about disclosing their HIV status to the entire household at once?

options.A: Announcing the diagnosis publicly at a large community gathering
options.B: Never telling anyone under any circumstances whatsoever
options.C: Leaving an anonymous note on the family dining table
options.D: Gradual disclosure, beginning with a single trusted relative

explanation: Starting with one supportive confidant helps build a safety net before expanding disclosure to wider family members. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h6)

question: Which factor must be carefully evaluated before a patient discloses their status to high-risk family members?

options.A: Potential risks of abandonment, domestic discord, or severe emotional backlash
options.B: The number of outpatient clinics operating in the local government area
options.C: The current market price of locally produced food supplements
options.D: The exact brand of antiretroviral medication prescribed by the clinic

explanation: Safety and emotional well-being are paramount; anticipating negative reactions allows the healthcare team to prepare appropriate support. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h6)

question: What is a primary responsibility of the nurse in implementing family-centered HIV care?

options.A: Legally enforcing mandatory quarantine for all infected household members
options.B: Assessing household dynamics and providing targeted health education
options.C: Prescribing specialized antiretroviral drug regimens independently
options.D: Purchasing all household groceries using personal nursing funds

explanation: Nurses evaluate home environments and educate relatives to empower them as effective partners in patient care. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h7)

question: Why is facilitating confidential family conferences in the clinic setting beneficial?

options.A: It replaces the need for individual patient consultations entirely
options.B: It forces family members to share their personal medical histories publicly
options.C: It prevents patients from speaking directly with the attending physician
options.D: It gives relatives a safe space to ask questions and align on realistic care plans

explanation: Structured conferences clear up misconceptions and foster collaborative support tailored to the patient's home environment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T6#GNS216_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary psychological response typically observed immediately following a new diagnosis of HIV?

options.A: Aggression and hostility
options.B: Indifference and apathy
options.C: Relief and acceptance
options.D: Shock, fear, and grief

explanation: A new diagnosis of a chronic, stigmatized illness typically triggers intense emotional shock, fear for the future, and grief over lost health. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h1)

question: How do support groups primarily help mitigate the immediate psychosocial impact of an HIV diagnosis?

options.A: By offering financial loans for medication procurement
options.B: By creating a safe, non-judgmental space to reduce social isolation
options.C: By curing the underlying viral load through collective energy
options.D: By replacing the need for professional psychiatric medication

explanation: Peer support addresses the profound isolation and fear of judgment by providing a community of individuals sharing similar lived experiences. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h1)

question: Which support model is specifically facilitated by individuals who are also living with the virus and share their experiential wisdom?

options.A: Primary Physician Roundtables
options.B: Clinically Integrated Groups
options.C: Surgical Recovery Guilds
options.D: Peer-Led Support Circles

explanation: Peer-led circles rely on veteran members who have lived experience with HIV to guide and mentor newer participants. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h2)

question: Why are adolescent and youth-focused support clubs particularly valuable in HIV management?

options.A: They replace parental guidance entirely with medical directives
options.B: They focus exclusively on curing opportunistic infections in children
options.C: They eliminate the need for antiretroviral therapy during school hours
options.D: They address unique challenges like disclosure, peer pressure, and transition to adult care

explanation: Young people face distinct developmental hurdles, such as navigating romantic relationships and moving from pediatric to adult clinics, which youth clubs target directly. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h2)

question: What is the primary medication-related goal supported by peer accountability in HIV support groups?

options.A: Reduction of medication acquisition costs
options.B: Substitution of prescription drugs with herbal remedies
options.C: Sustained adherence to antiretroviral therapy
options.D: Immediate elimination of all drug side effects

explanation: Support groups foster routine consistency and peer encouragement, which directly drives long-term adherence to antiretroviral medications. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h3)

question: A patient frequently forgets their evening dose of antiretroviral medication due to a busy work schedule. Which intervention typically practiced in a support group would best assist this patient?

options.A: Relying solely on clinic nurses to call every evening
options.B: Switching entirely to intravenous medication administration
options.C: Sharing practical routine-building strategies like pairing doses with meals or setting alarms
options.D: Stopping the medication temporarily until the schedule clears

explanation: Peers frequently share actionable lifestyle modifications, such as pairing pill-taking with daily habits, to solve adherence barriers. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary psychological transformation that occurs when individuals participate in supportive peer environments regarding their diagnosis?

options.A: Replacement of shame with shared solidarity
options.B: Development of indifference toward health outcomes
options.C: Isolation from all family members
options.D: Complete denial of the medical condition

explanation: Support groups actively counter shame and stigma by fostering a sense of shared community and mutual acceptance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h4)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct outcome of combating internalized stigma through peer support?

options.A: Complete eradication of the global viral reservoir
options.B: Restoration of personal self-worth
options.C: Open discussion of treatment regimens
options.D: Empowerment to challenge community discrimination

explanation: While peer support improves individual coping and social empowerment, it does not biologically eradicate the global viral reservoir. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h4)

question: What initial step must a nurse take before referring a patient to an HIV support group?

options.A: Mandating public disclosure of the patient's status to the community
options.B: Conducting a comprehensive assessment of emotional readiness and support systems
options.C: Filing a legal consent waiver with the local government
options.D: Withholding antiretroviral drugs until group attendance is confirmed

explanation: A thorough nursing assessment ensures that referrals match the individual's specific psychological state and readiness for group interaction. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h5)

question: Why is it important for nurses to address confidentiality fears before a patient attends their first support group?

options.A: To legally bind the nurse to pay for transport costs
options.B: To replace the need for hospital-based medical charts
options.C: To reduce anxiety and increase the likelihood of successful group engagement
options.D: To prevent the patient from ever taking medications again

explanation: Fear of accidental disclosure or gossip is a major barrier to participation; addressing these concerns builds trust and encourages attendance. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h5)

question: Which clinical metric is commonly tracked to evaluate the biological success of support group interventions?

options.A: Total body height measurements
options.B: Frequency of dental checkups
options.C: Daily caloric intake volume
options.D: Viral load suppression rates

explanation: Viral load suppression is a key clinical indicator of successful antiretroviral adherence and overall treatment efficacy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h6)

question: What type of data do pharmacy refill rates provide when assessing support group outcomes?

options.A: Economic data detailing national inflation rates
options.B: Psychological data measuring depression severity
options.C: Genetical data tracking viral mutations
options.D: Behavioral data regarding treatment adherence

explanation: Pharmacy refill tracking provides concrete behavioral evidence of how consistently patients are collecting their prescribed medications over time. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T7#GNS216_U6_T7_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of HIV counselling in a clinical setting?

options.A: To isolate infected individuals from the general population
options.B: To determine the exact timeline of viral transmission
options.C: To facilitate informed decision-making and risk assessment
options.D: To fulfill mandatory legal requirements for employment

explanation: Counselling creates a safe space for clients to understand their risks, weigh testing options, and prepare for potential results. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h1)

question: Why is HIV disclosure considered a critical component of long-term patient management?

options.A: It automatically guarantees financial aid from the government
options.B: It removes the legal obligation to use barrier methods
options.C: It completely eliminates the possibility of future reinfection
options.D: It supports adherence to antiretroviral therapy and social support

explanation: Sharing one's status helps build a reliable support system, which is vital for maintaining daily medication routines and emotional well-being. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h1)

question: Which principle must guide every pre-test counselling session?

options.A: Voluntary participation
options.B: Mandatory family involvement
options.C: Financial clearance
options.D: Immediate partner notification

explanation: Testing must always be voluntary, empowering the client to make an autonomous choice about their health. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary benefit of discussing potential results during pre-test counselling?

options.A: It eliminates all anxiety regarding needles
options.B: It speeds up laboratory processing times
options.C: It diagnoses opportunistic infections early
options.D: It prepares the client emotionally for any outcome

explanation: Anticipating the emotional impact beforehand helps clients process the actual result more effectively when it is delivered. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h2)

question: What is the primary focus of post-test counselling for an individual who tests negative?

options.A: Immediate initiation of antiretroviral drugs
options.B: Risk-reduction strategies and prevention education
options.C: Contact tracing of previous sexual partners
options.D: Mandatory disclosure to family members

explanation: Negative results provide an ideal educational window to reinforce safe practices and explain the concept of the diagnostic window period. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h3)

question: A client receives a newly confirmed HIV-positive result and appears visibly shaken. What is the most appropriate immediate action for the nurse?

options.A: Hand over the prescription and discharge the client quickly
options.B: Ask for the names of all past sexual partners right away
options.C: Refer the client to a psychiatric hospital for admission
options.D: Provide immediate emotional support and allow time to process

explanation: New diagnoses often trigger acute emotional shock; pausing to offer support and space is essential before piling on logistical details. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h3)

question: What does HIV disclosure primarily involve?

options.A: Registering for specialized workplace insurance schemes
options.B: Reporting infectious disease statistics to the government
options.C: Sharing one's positive serostatus with selected individuals
options.D: Publishing medical records in public health registries

explanation: Disclosure refers to the voluntary or planned communication of one's HIV diagnosis to partners, family, or support networks. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h4)

question: How does successful disclosure directly impact clinical treatment outcomes?

options.A: It removes the need for routine viral load monitoring
options.B: It prevents the development of opportunistic fungal infections
options.C: It guarantees complete eradication of the virus from the body
options.D: It improves antiretroviral medication adherence by reducing secrecy

explanation: When patients do not have to hide their medication, taking pills daily becomes easier, supporting consistent adherence. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h4)

question: Which factor is most commonly reported as the primary barrier to HIV disclosure?

options.A: Lack of available transportation to clinics
options.B: Fear of stigma and discrimination
options.C: Inability to understand medical terminology
options.D: Preference for traditional herbal remedies

explanation: Societal prejudice and anticipated negative reactions heavily deter individuals from openly sharing their diagnosis. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h5)

question: Why might a female client in a resource-limited setting hesitate to disclose her status to her husband?

options.A: She plans to stop taking her medications entirely
options.B: She fears experiencing physical violence or abandonment
options.C: She is legally prohibited from discussing lab results
options.D: Her husband is automatically immune to viral infections

explanation: Economic and social dependency can make disclosure perilous if the partner reacts with hostility, abuse, or abandonment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h5)

question: What is the defining feature of provider-assisted partner notification?

options.A: Partners are tested without their knowledge during routine care
options.B: Clients are forced to disclose within twenty-four hours
options.C: The government publishes the names of infected individuals
options.D: Healthcare staff contact partners directly with the client's consent

explanation: Provider referral involves trained personnel reaching out to contacts confidentially, protecting the original client's privacy. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: Under what circumstance is contract referral typically utilized during counselling?

options.A: When the client refuses to test anyone else in the household
options.B: When the client needs a defined timeframe to attempt disclosure independently before staff intervene
options.C: When the client requests police intervention immediately
options.D: When the laboratory loses the initial blood sample results

explanation: Contract referral gives the client an agreed-upon window to tell their partner themselves, with backup from the clinic if they fail. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h6)

question: What is a major benefit of connecting a newly diagnosed client to an HIV peer support group?

options.A: It replaces the need for antiretroviral medications
options.B: It offers visible proof of healthy long-term survival
options.C: It legally exempts them from workplace screening
options.D: It provides free laboratory diagnostic testing on-site

explanation: Seeing peers living well with HIV helps dispel fear and provides practical coping strategies for daily life. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h7)

question: A client expresses severe hopelessness and withdraws from communication following a positive test result. What nursing intervention is most appropriate?

options.A: Immediately discontinue all scheduled clinic appointments
options.B: Scold the client for having a negative attitude
options.C: Advise the client to keep the diagnosis entirely secret
options.D: Provide ongoing psychosocial support and assess for mental health needs

explanation: Severe hopelessness indicates deep psychological distress requiring empathetic support and potential referral for specialized mental health care. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h7)

question: What does medical confidentiality require of a nurse handling HIV test results?

options.A: Protecting patient information from unauthorized disclosure
options.B: Sharing results with family members to ensure compliance
options.C: Reporting positive cases directly to local employers
options.D: Publishing case logs on community bulletin boards

explanation: Confidentiality dictates that patient health information remains strictly between the clinician and the client unless proper consent is given. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a protected right under the Nigerian HIV/AIDS Anti-Discrimination Act?

options.A: The right to demand free housing from healthcare employers
options.B: Protection against mandatory workplace testing
options.C: Protection from discrimination in educational institutions
options.D: Freedom from unfair employment termination based on status

explanation: The Act protects against discrimination, mandatory testing, and unlawful termination, but it does not mandate the provision of free housing. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T8#GNS216_U6_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary function of HIV Counselling and Testing within healthcare systems?

options.A: Serving as the gateway to prevention, care, and treatment
options.B: Replacing routine diagnostic blood screening in laboratories
options.C: Providing permanent immunity against secondary infections
options.D: Enforcing mandatory isolation for infected individuals

explanation: HCT acts as the vital first contact point connecting individuals to life-saving medical care and preventive interventions. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h1)

question: Provider-initiated testing and counseling differs from traditional voluntary testing because healthcare workers:

options.A: Restrict testing exclusively to pregnant women
options.B: Actively recommend the test as part of standard clinical care
options.C: Perform the procedure without any form of verbal consent
options.D: Mandate lifelong quarantine for positive diagnoses

explanation: Provider-initiated approaches involve clinicians suggesting the test routinely during patient visits to reduce stigma and catch infections early. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h1)

question: Which principle ensures that a client agrees to an HIV test freely without coercion or pressure?

options.A: Anonymous tracking
options.B: Systemic reporting
options.C: Informed consent
options.D: Mandatory compliance

explanation: Consent guarantees that participation in testing is entirely voluntary and based on a clear understanding of the process. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h2)

question: Maintaining strict privacy regarding a client's test results aligns with which core HCT principle?

options.A: Public transparency
options.B: Institutional auditing
options.C: Epidemiological mapping
options.D: Confidentiality

explanation: Confidentiality protects personal health data from unauthorized disclosure, encouraging individuals to seek testing without fear of social repercussions. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h2)

question: Why is discussing the window period an essential part of pre-test counseling?

options.A: It determines the precise dosage of antiretroviral medications needed
options.B: It establishes the financial cost of laboratory confirmation tests
options.C: It calculates the exact date the client contracted the virus
options.D: It explains why a very recent exposure might yield a false negative result

explanation: The window period represents the time before antibodies develop, meaning a negative test during this phase does not entirely rule out recent infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h3)

question: What is a primary goal of the pre-test counseling session?

options.A: Initiating lifelong antiretroviral drug therapy immediately
options.B: Reporting the client's personal details to local law enforcement
options.C: Issuing a formal certificate of viral clearance
options.D: Assessing personal risk and obtaining informed consent

explanation: Pre-test sessions focus on evaluating risk factors, preparing the client, and ensuring they agree voluntarily to the procedure. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h3)

question: What is the purpose of a tie-breaker test in an HIV testing algorithm?

options.A: To test for opportunistic infections alongside HIV
options.B: To replace the initial screening test during routine check-ups
options.C: To measure the exact viral load circulating in the bloodstream
options.D: To resolve discordant results between the first and second assays

explanation: A tie-breaker test is introduced when the screening and confirmatory rapid tests give conflicting or discordant outcomes. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h4)

question: A client's initial screening assay is reactive, but their second confirmatory assay is non-reactive. What does this outcome indicate?

options.A: Complete immunity to future viral exposures
options.B: Definitive confirmation of an HIV-positive status
options.C: An expired rapid diagnostic kit batch
options.D: Discordant results requiring a tie-breaker assay

explanation: Conflicting outcomes between the first two assays mean the diagnostic algorithm requires a third tie-breaker test for clarity. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h4)

question: Which action is most appropriate during post-test counseling for a client with a negative HIV result?

options.A: Reporting the negative test to local public health registries
options.B: Prescribing a standard regimen of antiretroviral drugs
options.C: Isolating the client to prevent future exposure risks
options.D: Providing targeted risk-reduction education and prevention strategies

explanation: A negative result serves as an educational opportunity to discuss prevention methods and maintain a safe status. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h5)

question: A client who engages in ongoing high-risk activities tests negative for HIV. What should the nurse emphasize regarding future testing?

options.A: Testing is only required if severe physical symptoms appear
options.B: They are permanently immune and never need testing again
options.C: Periodic re-testing is necessary due to potential window period exposures
options.D: Antibody levels will remain undetectable for the rest of their life

explanation: Continuous exposure risks mean a single negative test only reflects status up to the window period, requiring ongoing screening. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h5)

question: How should a nurse manage a client's immediate emotional shock following an HIV-positive diagnosis?

options.A: List all potential opportunistic infections to warn them of danger
options.B: Provide a calm, empathetic space and allow time to process the news
options.C: Immediately discharge the client to prevent clinic overcrowding
options.D: Demand immediate names of all sexual partners for contact tracing

explanation: Emotional shock requires patience, reassurance, and a supportive environment before moving into complex treatment details. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h6)

question: What is assisted partner notification in the context of HIV management?

options.A: A legal mandate forcing public broadcast of positive diagnoses
options.B: A laboratory procedure to cross-check blood sample integrity
options.C: A voluntary service helping clients notify their sexual partners safely
options.D: An automated messaging system run by insurance companies

explanation: Assisted partner notification supports clients in informing their partners while minimizing risks of violence or abandonment. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h6)

question: Routine opt-out testing for pregnant women is a core component of which specialized program?

options.A: Adolescent reproductive health initiatives
options.B: Prevention of mother-to-child transmission
options.C: Occupational post-exposure prophylaxis
options.D: Community mass screening campaigns

explanation: PMTCT programs prioritize routine antenatal screening to catch maternal infections early and prevent vertical transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h7)

question: Which barrier frequently discourages adolescents from seeking independent HIV testing services?

options.A: Mandatory lifetime hospitalization upon initial screening
options.B: Immunity to viral infections due to young physiological age
options.C: Fear of stigma and concerns regarding confidentiality breaches
options.D: An absolute lack of physical testing kits in urban hospitals

explanation: Young people often avoid testing facilities out of anxiety that their status might be exposed to parents, peers, or community members. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h7)

question: Which of the following practices is NOT ethically permissible in standard HIV testing protocols?

options.A: Safeguarding diagnostic records in locked filing cabinets or secure databases
options.B: Offering voluntary screening during routine antenatal care visits
options.C: Providing pre-test counseling before collecting a blood sample
options.D: Conducting mandatory testing without the client's informed consent

explanation: Forcing a client to undergo testing without voluntary informed consent violates foundational medical ethics and human rights laws. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h8)

question: What ethical challenge do nurses frequently navigate when managing HIV client records?

options.A: Publishing patient names in local newspapers for transparency
options.B: Balancing individual confidentiality rights with public health safety
options.C: Deciding whether to destroy medical files after one week
options.D: Sharing diagnostic findings freely with casual acquaintances

explanation: Nurses must strictly protect patient privacy while remaining mindful of legal obligations regarding serious public health risks. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T10#GNS216_U6_T10_h8)

question: What is the approximate baseline risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV without any medical interventions?
explanation: Without any prophylactic or therapeutic interventions, the natural rate of vertical transmission from an infected mother to her child typically falls between 15% and 45%. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h1)

question: During which physiological period does the highest risk of intrapartum HIV transmission typically occur?

options.A: During the first trimester of pregnancy
options.B: During the first week after weaning
options.C: During the actual birth process
options.D: During conception and fertilization

explanation: Intrapartum transmission happens primarily during labor and delivery due to the infant's direct contact with maternal blood and infectious vaginal secretions. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h1)

question: Which prong of the PMTCT strategy focuses specifically on preventing unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV?

options.A: Prong 4
options.B: Prong 1
options.C: Prong 2
options.D: Prong 3

explanation: Prong 2 of the global PMTCT framework is dedicated to preventing unintended pregnancies among women who are already living with HIV through voluntary family planning. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h2)

question: What is the primary objective of Prong 1 in the comprehensive PMTCT framework?

options.A: Stopping primary HIV infection in women of childbearing age
options.B: Ensuring exclusive formula feeding for all exposed infants
options.C: Managing opportunistic infections in HIV-positive fathers
options.D: Providing immediate postnatal antiretroviral syrup to newborns

explanation: Prong 1 targets the general population of women of childbearing age to stop them from acquiring HIV in the first place, thereby preventing subsequent vertical transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h2)

question: What does the Option B-Plus strategy entail for pregnant women diagnosed with HIV?

options.A: Temporary ART initiated only during the third trimester
options.B: Dual therapy given strictly during active labor and delivery
options.C: Prophylactic vitamins and exclusive monitoring without drugs
options.D: Lifelong antiretroviral therapy regardless of CD4 count

explanation: Option B-Plus mandates that every pregnant or breastfeeding woman with HIV starts lifelong antiretroviral therapy immediately upon diagnosis, irrespective of her current CD4 cell count. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h3)

question: Why is opt-out HIV counseling and testing recommended as the standard during initial antenatal visits?

options.A: It replaces the requirement for routine physical examinations.
options.B: It ensures maximum case identification and timely intervention.
options.C: It forces every patient to accept medical treatment legally.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any subsequent laboratory blood work.

explanation: Routine opt-out testing reduces stigma and catches undiagnosed infections early, allowing prompt initiation of ART to suppress maternal viral load before delivery. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h3)

question: A pregnant woman living with HIV presents in active labor with a high, unsuppressed viral load. Which obstetric intervention is most likely to reduce the risk of vertical transmission?

options.A: Delaying maternal antiretroviral therapy until after delivery
options.B: Utilizing internal fetal scalp electrode monitoring
options.C: Performing an artificial rupture of membranes immediately
options.D: Scheduling or performing an elective cesarean section

explanation: For women with high viral loads, an elective cesarean section performed before labor starts significantly lowers the infant's contact with infectious maternal fluids. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h4)

question: Which of the following interventions should be avoided during the labor of an HIV-positive woman to prevent direct trauma to the fetus?

options.A: Monitoring maternal vital signs every two hours
options.B: Continuous maternal oral antiretroviral therapy
options.C: Administration of prescribed prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Internal fetal scalp electrode monitoring

explanation: Internal fetal monitoring breaks the fetal skin barrier, creating a direct portal of entry for the virus from maternal fluids, and should be avoided. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h4)

question: Which diagnostic test is used to detect HIV infection in an infant born to an HIV-positive mother at 6 weeks of age?

options.A: DNA Polymerase Chain Reaction using dried blood spots
options.B: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay antibody test
options.C: Rapid whole-blood antibody screening cassette
options.D: Western blot confirmatory serum antibody assay

explanation: Infants possess maternal antibodies up to 18 months, rendering standard antibody tests unreliable; therefore, DNA PCR testing via dried blood spots is required. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h5)

question: What is the primary clinical purpose of administering prophylactic antiretroviral syrup to a newborn immediately after birth?

options.A: To cure any established congenital HIV infection permanently
options.B: To prevent viral replication if transmission occurred intrapartum
options.C: To destroy maternal antibodies circulating in infant plasma
options.D: To stimulate the infant's immature bone marrow immune response

explanation: Postnatal infant prophylaxis provides pre-emptive systemic drug coverage to stop any virus acquired during birth from successfully establishing chronic infection. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h5)

question: Why is mixed feeding (giving breast milk and water or formula) strongly discouraged for mothers living on ART?

options.A: It completely stops the natural production of breast milk.
options.B: It destroys maternal antiretroviral drugs in the breast milk.
options.C: It damages infant gut mucosa and increases transmission risk.
options.D: It causes immediate allergic anaphylaxis in newborn infants.

explanation: Introducing non-breast milk liquids or foods irritates and compromises the immature intestinal lining, making it much easier for the virus in breast milk to cross into the infant bloodstream. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h6)

question: What is the recommended duration of exclusive breastfeeding for an HIV-positive mother on suppressive antiretroviral therapy under current guidelines?

options.A: First 6 months of life
options.B: First 12 months of life
options.C: First 24 months of life
options.D: First 6 weeks of life

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months, after which nutritionally adequate complementary foods should be introduced alongside continued breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T11#GNS216_U6_T11_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of infant feeding guidelines in the context of maternal HIV?

options.A: Ensuring immediate cessation of all lactation
options.B: Eliminating all maternal nutritional requirements
options.C: Maximizing HIV-free survival of the infant
options.D: Promoting exclusive formula feeding universally

explanation: The overarching objective is to keep the infant nourished and free from the virus while protecting maternal health. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h1)

question: Without any interventions, what is the approximate baseline risk range of mother-to-child transmission of HIV?

options.A: 1 to 5 percent
options.B: 80 to 95 percent
options.C: 50 to 75 percent
options.D: 15 to 45 percent

explanation: In the absence of prophylactic interventions like antiretroviral therapy, the virus can be transmitted during gestation, delivery, or breastfeeding within this statistical range. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h1)

question: How long does the World Health Organization recommend exclusive breastfeeding for infants born to mothers with HIV who are on antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: First three months of life
options.B: Until twenty-four months of age
options.C: First six months of life
options.D: Until twelve months of age

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the initial six months, after which safe complementary foods are introduced. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h2)

question: Why did global health guidelines shift from universally advising against breastfeeding to supporting it alongside maternal antiretroviral therapy?

options.A: Due to the high cost of manufactured formula in urban centers
options.B: To eliminate the need for infant HIV diagnostic testing
options.C: To reduce infant mortality from malnutrition and contaminated water associated with replacement feeding
options.D: Because breast milk completely neutralizes the virus within forty-eight hours

explanation: While artificial feeding prevented HIV transmission, unsafe water and poor nutrition caused fatal diarrheal diseases, prompting a balanced risk-benefit approach. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h2)

question: What does exclusive breastfeeding mean in clinical practice?

options.A: Providing breast milk supplemented with cereal water
options.B: Alternating breast milk with glucose water every four hours
options.C: Combining breast milk with small amounts of diluted formula
options.D: Giving only breast milk with no other liquids or solids

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding prohibits water, ritual drinks, or food, ensuring the infant gut is exposed solely to the protective properties of breast milk. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h3)

question: A nursing mother living with HIV reports cracked nipples and mild breast pain. What is the most critical clinical concern?

options.A: Complete neutralization of antiretroviral drugs in the mother's bloodstream
options.B: Increased risk of viral shedding into the breast milk due to localized inflammation
options.C: Immediate development of systemic infant thrush
options.D: Permanent cessation of milk production in the affected breast

explanation: Inflammatory conditions like mastitis or nipple trauma increase viral load in breast milk, elevating the risk of vertical transmission. [learn more](GNS216_U6_T12#GNS216_U6_T12_h3)
