question: Why is a thorough grasp of normal maternal physiology essential for nurses in antenatal care settings?

options.A: To accurately predict the exact delivery date without ultrasound imaging
options.B: To prevent the misdiagnosis of normal gestational variants as pathological conditions
options.C: To completely halt all natural hormonal shifts during the first trimester
options.D: To eliminate the need for routine maternal blood pressure monitoring

explanation: Many normal pregnancy changes mimic disease signs, so nurses must recognize them as healthy adaptations to avoid unnecessary anxiety or interventions. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h1)

question: What causes physiological anemia in pregnant women?

options.A: Severe bone marrow suppression caused by elevated progesterone
options.B: Plasma volume increases proportionally much more than red blood cell mass
options.C: Complete cessation of iron absorption in the small intestine
options.D: Sudden destruction of erythrocytes by placental antibodies

explanation: The blood becomes diluted because fluid volume expands significantly faster than cellular components, leading to a lower hemoglobin concentration. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h2)

question: A woman in her third trimester feels dizzy, pale, and nauseated while lying flat on her back during a clinic examination. What is the most likely physiological cause?

options.A: Acute elevation of systemic vascular resistance causing cerebral ischemia
options.B: Sudden spike in maternal red blood cell mass triggering hyperviscosity
options.C: Complete occlusion of the abdominal aorta by fetal movement
options.D: Compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus reducing venous return

explanation: Supine hypotension syndrome occurs when the heavy uterus blocks blood return to the heart, dropping cardiac output and blood pressure. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h2)

question: What is the primary mechanism responsible for maternal hyperventilation during gestation?

options.A: Direct physical stretching of the intercostal muscles by the ribs
options.B: Mechanical obstruction of the upper airway by soft tissue edema
options.C: Progesterone acting centrally on the brainstem to alter carbon dioxide thresholds
options.D: A compensatory response to severe primary metabolic alkalosis

explanation: Elevated progesterone sensitizes the respiratory center, causing deeper and more frequent breathing even when oxygen levels are normal. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h3)

question: Which pulmonary volume typically decreases during pregnancy due to the upward displacement of the diaphragm?

options.A: Tidal volume
options.B: Minute ventilation
options.C: Functional residual capacity
options.D: Respiratory rate

explanation: The upward push of the uterus reduces the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal breath, which explains why pregnant women desaturate faster during airway emergencies. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h3)

question: How does the glomerular filtration rate typically change during a normal pregnancy?

options.A: It increases significantly by up to fifty percent
options.B: It fluctuates wildly depending on the time of day
options.C: It decreases steadily to conserve essential electrolytes
options.D: It remains entirely unchanged throughout all three trimesters

explanation: The kidneys work harder to clear waste products, which elevates the glomerular filtration rate early in the first trimester. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h4)

question: Why are pregnant women particularly susceptible to ascending urinary tract infections?

options.A: A permanent alkaline shift in total body pH balance
options.B: Progesterone-induced ureteral dilation and urinary stasis
options.C: Reduced renal plasma flow slowing down bacterial clearance
options.D: Complete destruction of the bladder mucosa by fetal hormones

explanation: When urine flow slows down through relaxed, widened ureters, bacteria can easily multiply and ascend toward the kidneys. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h4)

question: What is the primary cause of heartburn and delayed gastric emptying in pregnant women?

options.A: Hypersecretion of hydrochloric acid by the parietal cells of the stomach
options.B: Physical blockage of the pyloric sphincter by the growing fetal head
options.C: Progesterone-induced smooth muscle relaxation throughout the digestive tract
options.D: Excessive consumption of highly spiced traditional foods

explanation: Progesterone relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle, slowing down food transit and allowing stomach acids to slip back into the esophagus. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h5)

question: Why does the maternal body develop peripheral insulin resistance during the later stages of gestation?

options.A: To prevent the mother from storing any excess fat reserves for lactation
options.B: To accelerate maternal bone mineralization and prevent dental caries
options.C: To compensate for a sudden and dangerous drop in pancreatic insulin production
options.D: To ensure a continuous, adequate supply of glucose crosses the placenta to the fetus

explanation: By making maternal cells less responsive to insulin, more glucose remains circulating in the blood available for active fetal uptake. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h5)

question: Which hormone is responsible for maintaining the corpus luteum during the early weeks of gestation?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Prolactin
options.C: Human chorionic gonadotropin
options.D: Human placental lactogen

explanation: Human chorionic gonadotropin signals the corpus luteum to continue producing progesterone until the placenta is fully functional. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h6)

question: What is a major immunological function of elevated maternal cortisol levels during pregnancy?

options.A: Suppressing maternal immune responses to prevent rejection of the fetus
options.B: Directly stimulating the fetal bone marrow to produce erythrocytes
options.C: Enhancing uterine muscle contractions in preparation for normal labor
options.D: Accelerating the breakdown of maternal red blood cells

explanation: Higher cortisol helps modulate the maternal immune system so it tolerates the genetically distinct fetal tissue as an allograft. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h6)

question: Which hormone contributes significantly to the softening of pelvic ligaments and joints during pregnancy?

options.A: Aldosterone
options.B: Calcitonin
options.C: Vasopressin
options.D: Relaxin

explanation: Relaxin loosens pelvic connective tissue and joints to accommodate passage of the baby through the birth canal. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h7)

question: What is the primary mechanical reason for the development of lordosis in late pregnancy?

options.A: The forward shift in the maternal center of gravity caused by the growing uterus
options.B: Severe calcium depletion leading to softening of the vertebrae
options.C: A sudden increase in bone density throughout the axial skeleton
options.D: Spasms of the lower abdominal wall muscles caused by stretching

explanation: As the abdomen pushes forward, the mother leans back to maintain balance, creating an exaggerated inward curve in the lower spine. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h7)

question: Which set of symptoms should a nurse teach a pregnant woman to report immediately as potential warning signs of pre-eclampsia?

options.A: Severe headache, visual disturbances, and sudden facial swelling
options.B: Mild dependent ankle edema at the end of a long day
options.C: Mild heartburn relieved by simple antacids and small meals
options.D: Infrequent Braxton Hicks contractions without cervical change

explanation: Headaches, vision changes, and sudden swelling above the waist are classic red flags for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h8)

question: What practical positioning advice should a nurse give to a pregnant woman experiencing dizziness and faintness while resting in bed?

options.A: Lie strictly in a lateral side-lying position to relieve vena caval compression
options.B: Lie completely flat on the back with legs elevated above the heart
options.C: Sleep in a completely prone position with a pillow under the abdomen
options.D: Stand up quickly and walk around to stimulate venous return from the legs

explanation: Side-lying shifts the weight of the uterus off the major blood vessels, instantly restoring cardiac output and relieving dizziness. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T003#GNS226_U2_T003_h8)

question: What defines a dizygotic multiple pregnancy?

options.A: Fertilization of two separate ova by two spermatozoa
options.B: Implantation of two embryos from separate maternal cycles
options.C: Division of a single fertilized ovum into two embryos
options.D: Spontaneous division of the blastocyst after four weeks

explanation: Dizygotic pregnancies occur when two separate eggs are released and fertilized by two different sperm cells, creating fraternal twins. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h1)

question: Why do monozygotic twins share identical genetic material?

options.A: They receive double genetic input from the maternal side
options.B: They inherit identical genes from two separate sperm cells
options.C: They share the exact same placental circulation
options.D: They develop from a single fertilized ovum that splits

explanation: Because monozygotic twins originate from one single zygote that divides early in development, they carry the exact same genetic blueprint. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h1)

question: Which placentation type carries the highest risk of umbilical cord entanglement?

options.A: Dichorionic diamniotic
options.B: Monochorionic diamniotic
options.C: Monochorionic monoamniotic
options.D: Dichorionic monoamniotic

explanation: In a monochorionic monoamniotic pregnancy, fetuses share the same amniotic cavity without a dividing membrane, making cord entanglement a major fatal hazard. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h2)

question: A first-trimester ultrasound reveals a lambda sign between two gestational sacs. What is the correct placentation classification?

options.A: Monochorionic monoamniotic
options.B: Dichorionic monoamniotic
options.C: Monochorionic diamniotic
options.D: Dichorionic diamniotic

explanation: The lambda sign, or twin peak sign, is a triangular projection of tissue extending into the inter-twin membrane base, diagnostic of dichorionicity. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h2)

question: What is the primary diagnostic tool used to confirm a multiple pregnancy and determine chorionicity?

options.A: Abdominal palpation
options.B: Serum hCG titers
options.C: Ultrasonography
options.D: Auscultation of fetal hearts

explanation: Ultrasound imaging is the definitive method to visualize multiple gestational sacs, embryos, and membrane structures early in pregnancy. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h3)

question: Why do women with multiple pregnancies require more frequent antenatal visits than those with singletons?

options.A: To ensure the mother takes her routine daily iron supplements
options.B: To schedule elective operative deliveries at 32 weeks
options.C: To prevent the natural onset of spontaneous dizygotic twinning
options.D: To monitor for rapid development of maternal and fetal complications

explanation: The elevated physiological load and high risk of conditions like pre-eclampsia and growth restriction necessitate rigorous, close monitoring. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h3)

question: What is the most common cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality in multiple pregnancies?

options.A: Prematurity
options.B: Twin reversed arterial perfusion
options.C: Neonatal jaundice
options.D: Congenital heart disease

explanation: Most multiple pregnancies end in preterm delivery, putting newborns at risk of respiratory distress syndrome and other prematurity complications. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h4)

question: Which maternal complication is particularly common following the birth of multiple fetuses due to uterine overdistention?

options.A: Placental accreta spectrum
options.B: Postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Gestational epilepsy
options.D: Chronic renal failure

explanation: Overstretched uterine muscles often fail to contract effectively after delivery, leading to uterine atony and heavy postpartum bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h4)

question: Which micronutrient supplementation is especially crucial in multiple pregnancies to prevent severe maternal anemia?

options.A: Potassium
options.B: Vitamin C
options.C: Vitamin K
options.D: Iron

explanation: The expanded blood volume and demands of multiple fetuses drastically increase the risk of iron-deficiency anemia, making iron supplements essential. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h5)

question: How should maternal caloric intake be managed during a twin pregnancy compared to a singleton pregnancy?

options.A: Increased significantly to match the metabolic needs of each fetus
options.B: Supplemented exclusively with high-protein shakes rather than whole foods
options.C: Maintained at baseline levels because nutrient absorption doubles automatically
options.D: Restricted to prevent excessive maternal weight gain and gestational diabetes

explanation: Mothers carrying multiples require higher daily caloric and nutrient intake to support optimal fetal growth and prevent maternal depletion. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h5)

question: What is a mandatory requirement immediately following the vaginal delivery of the first twin?

options.A: Assessment of the lie and presentation of the second twin
options.B: Administration of general anesthesia to the mother
options.C: Immediate clamping and removal of the shared placenta
options.D: Immediate discharge of the first twin to the postnatal ward

explanation: The midwife and doctor must check the position of the second twin right after the first baby is born to manage its delivery safely. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h6)

question: Why is active management of the third stage of labor critical in women who have delivered multiple babies?

options.A: To induce immediate lactation before the neonates are transferred
options.B: To prevent the spontaneous retention of the second twin's amniotic sac
options.C: To correct maternal electrolyte imbalances caused by prolonged labor
options.D: To mitigate the high risk of postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony

explanation: An overdistended uterus from multiple gestations contracts poorly after delivery, making active management essential to prevent life-threatening hemorrhage. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h6)

question: Which clinical parameter must be closely monitored in the immediate postpartum period to detect atony or retained products?

options.A: Fasting blood glucose levels
options.B: Uterine involution and lochia amount
options.C: Serum electrolyte balance
options.D: Maternal visual acuity and pupillary reflex

explanation: Checking the tone and size of the uterus along with monitoring vaginal bleeding helps catch postpartum hemorrhage early. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h7)

question: What is a major psychosocial risk for mothers during the immediate postpartum period following a multiple birth?

options.A: Postpartum depression and severe fatigue
options.B: Persistent postpartum psychosis linked to fetal genetics
options.C: Sudden permanent loss of maternal memory
options.D: Complete rejection of infant feeding responsibilities

explanation: The immense physical demands of caring for multiple newborns simultaneously place mothers at high risk for exhaustion and mood disorders. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T018#GNS226_U2_T018_h7)

question: What gestational age threshold is typically used to define hypertension specifically induced by pregnancy?

options.A: After 20 weeks of gestation
options.B: During the third trimester only
options.C: At any point during the first trimester
options.D: Prior to 12 weeks of gestation

explanation: Hypertension that presents after twenty weeks of pregnancy in a woman with previously normal blood pressure points toward pregnancy induced disorders rather than chronic hypertension. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h1)

question: What blood pressure readings confirm the diagnosis of hypertension in an expectant mother?

options.A: 120/80 mmHg or higher
options.B: 130/85 mmHg or higher
options.C: 140/90 mmHg or higher
options.D: 160/100 mmHg or higher

explanation: A threshold of 140 over 90 millimeters of mercury is the standard clinical benchmark used to define hypertension in pregnant individuals. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h1)

question: Which condition is characterized by new-onset seizures in a patient with preeclampsia?

options.A: Superimposed preeclampsia
options.B: Eclampsia
options.C: Chronic hypertension
options.D: Gestational hypertension

explanation: The development of generalized seizures in a woman who already has preeclampsia marks the transition to eclampsia, a critical obstetric emergency. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h2)

question: How does gestational hypertension differ fundamentally from preeclampsia?

options.A: Gestational hypertension is caused by pre-existing kidney disease.
options.B: Gestational hypertension requires immediate emergency delivery.
options.C: Gestational hypertension always occurs before the twentieth week of pregnancy.
options.D: Gestational hypertension lacks associated proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction.

explanation: While both conditions involve high blood pressure after twenty weeks, gestational hypertension does not present with protein in the urine or systemic organ damage. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h2)

question: What primary vascular failure initiates the pathology of pregnancy induced hypertension in the placenta?

options.A: Premature rupture of the placental membranes
options.B: Hypertrophy of the fetal chorionic villi
options.C: Excessive dilation of the umbilical cord vessels
options.D: Inadequate remodeling of maternal spiral arteries

explanation: Poor trophoblastic invasion leads to narrow, high-resistance spiral arteries, causing chronic placental ischemia which drives the disease process. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h3)

question: Why does widespread endothelial cell injury result in clinical hypertension and edema?

options.A: Endothelial destruction causes immediate failure of the cardiac ventricles.
options.B: Damaged endothelial cells trigger severe vasoconstriction and increase capillary permeability.
options.C: Endothelial damage stops the production of all red blood cells.
options.D: Injured vessels release excessive amounts of potassium into the bloodstream.

explanation: When the inner lining of blood vessels is injured, vessels constrict and leak fluid into the interstitial spaces, raising blood pressure and causing edema. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h3)

question: Which demographic factor is a well-established risk factor for developing pregnancy induced hypertension?

options.A: Male fetal gender
options.B: Multiparity with five previous births
options.C: Nulliparity
options.D: Advanced paternal age

explanation: First-time mothers consistently demonstrate a substantially higher incidence of hypertensive disorders during pregnancy compared to multiparous women. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h4)

question: Why does a multiple gestation pregnancy increase the likelihood of hypertensive disorders?

options.A: Twin pregnancies always result in gestational diabetes first.
options.B: Increased placental mass amplifies ischemic and angiogenic factors.
options.C: Multiple fetuses physically compress maternal heart valves.
options.D: Maternal blood volume remains abnormally low in twin gestations.

explanation: Carrying more than one fetus creates a larger placental load, increasing the release of harmful circulating factors linked to endothelial injury. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h4)

question: Which symptom reported by a pregnant patient is a classic warning sign of hepatic involvement in preeclampsia?

options.A: Lower abdominal cramping and pelvic pressure
options.B: Intermittent burning during urination
options.C: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain
options.D: Sharp pain radiating down the left leg

explanation: Liver involvement and swelling place tension on Glisson's capsule, presenting as pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastric region. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h5)

question: A nurse is assessing a patient with gestational hypertension. Which finding indicates disease progression to preeclampsia?

options.A: Development of thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes
options.B: Bilateral swelling of the feet after standing
options.C: A single blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg
options.D: An increase in fetal movement frequency

explanation: The onset of systemic laboratory abnormalities like low platelets or liver enzyme elevation confirms that gestational hypertension has progressed to preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h5)

question: At what blood pressure threshold are antihypertensive drugs typically initiated in severe hypertension during pregnancy?

options.A: 130/80 mmHg or higher
options.B: 140/90 mmHg or higher
options.C: 150/95 mmHg or higher
options.D: 160/110 mmHg or higher

explanation: Severe range blood pressures of 160 over 110 millimeters of mercury require prompt antihypertensive therapy to protect the mother from stroke. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for implementing expectant management in preterm preeclampsia without severe features?

options.A: To cure the underlying placental pathology before delivery
options.B: To allow the maternal kidneys to repair themselves completely
options.C: To promote further fetal growth and pulmonary maturation
options.D: To eliminate the need for future antihypertensive drugs

explanation: Delaying delivery when safe allows the fetus more time to develop, reducing the risks associated with extreme prematurity. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h6)

question: What medication is routinely administered to prevent and control seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia?

options.A: Phenytoin sodium
options.B: Diazepam
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the internationally recognized first-line drug used to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h7)

question: What is the specific pharmacological antidote kept at the bedside during magnesium sulfate therapy?

options.A: Protamine sulfate
options.B: Vitamin K
options.C: Naloxone hydrochloride
options.D: Calcium gluconate

explanation: Calcium gluconate acts directly to reverse the neuromuscular and respiratory depression caused by toxic levels of magnesium sulfate. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h7)

question: What acronym describes the serious complication featuring hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets?

options.A: TORCH
options.B: HELLP
options.C: ARDS
options.D: DIC

explanation: HELLP syndrome stands for Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets, representing a severe variant of preeclampsia. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h8)

question: Which long-term health risk should be discussed with women who have experienced pregnancy induced hypertension?

options.A: Absolute sterility in subsequent reproductive years
options.B: Increased lifetime risk of chronic hypertension and cardiovascular disease
options.C: Guaranteed development of type 1 diabetes mellitus in later life
options.D: Permanent impairment of cognitive brain function within five years

explanation: A history of pregnancy induced hypertension serves as an independent risk factor for future cardiovascular disease and chronic hypertension. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T019#GNS226_U2_T019_h8)

question: What is the standard gestational age range for a normal term delivery?

options.A: Exactly at 40 completed weeks
options.B: Between 40 and 44 completed weeks
options.C: Between 37 and 42 completed weeks
options.D: Between 30 and 36 completed weeks

explanation: Term labour is clinically defined as occurring anytime from the completion of 37 weeks up to 42 weeks of gestation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: Which characteristic is essential for a delivery to be officially classified as a normal labour?

options.A: Elective induction of contractions
options.B: Surgical rupture of membranes early
options.C: Breech presentation with assistance
options.D: Spontaneous vertex presentation

explanation: A normal labour requires the fetus to present head-first by the vertex spontaneously without complex surgical maneuvers. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h1)

question: What is the term for the blood-tinged mucus discharge that often precedes true labour?

options.A: Amniotic fluid leak
options.B: The bloody show
options.C: Cervical polyp
options.D: Braxton Hicks sign

explanation: The show consists of the mucous plug and a small amount of blood released when the cervix effaces and dilates. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: How do true labour contractions differ primarily from false labour contractions?

options.A: True contractions increase in frequency and intensity and cause cervical change
options.B: False contractions always begin with the rupture of membranes
options.C: True contractions completely disappear with hydration and bed rest
options.D: False contractions become stronger when the mother walks around

explanation: True labour contractions are progressive and lead to actual cervical dilation, unlike irregular false contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h2)

question: What event marks the official end of the first stage of labour?

options.A: Rupture of the membranes
options.B: Complete cervical dilation
options.C: Delivery of the baby
options.D: Expulsion of the placenta

explanation: The first stage begins with true contractions and ends when the cervix reaches full 10 centimeters dilation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: A parturient has just delivered a healthy newborn and is currently awaiting the delivery of the placenta. Which stage of labour is she experiencing?

options.A: Second stage
options.B: First stage
options.C: Fourth stage
options.D: Third stage

explanation: The third stage spans from the birth of the baby until the complete expulsion of the placenta and fetal membranes. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h3)

question: What is the cardinal movement where the fetal chin presses against its chest to reduce the head diameter?

options.A: Engagement
options.B: Flexion
options.C: Extension
options.D: Restitution

explanation: Flexion allows the smallest suboccipitobregmatic diameter of the fetal head to present to the maternal pelvis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: Why are the cardinal movements of labour necessary for a vaginal birth?

options.A: They ensure the placenta separates smoothly from the uterine wall
options.B: They allow the fetal head to adapt to the varying diameters of the pelvis
options.C: They prevent the premature rupture of the amniotic membranes
options.D: They stimulate the release of oxytocin from the posterior pituitary gland

explanation: Because the maternal pelvis changes shape at different levels, the fetus must perform specific maneuvers to fit through. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h4)

question: Which clinical tool is used during abdominal palpation to determine fetal presentation and position?

options.A: Apgar scoring chart
options.B: Pelvimeter scale
options.C: Partograph grid
options.D: Leopold's maneuvers

explanation: Leopold's maneuvers are a systematic method of abdominal palpation used to check the position, lie, and presentation of the fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for reviewing the antenatal card upon a woman's admission to the labour ward?

options.A: To schedule the exact time when the baby will be born
options.B: To identify pre-existing risk factors and baseline laboratory results
options.C: To calculate the total hospital bills for the delivery process
options.D: To determine the preferred naming ceremony date for the family

explanation: Antenatal records contain vital screening data like blood group, infections, and obstetric history that guide safe clinical management. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h5)

question: How often should the fetal heart rate be auscultated and recorded during the active phase of normal labour?

options.A: Every 2 hours
options.B: Every 30 minutes
options.C: Every 10 minutes
options.D: Once every hour

explanation: Routine intrapartum guidelines recommend listening to and recording the fetal heart rate every half hour during active first-stage labour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: What clinical action is indicated if a woman's cervical dilation curve on the partograph crosses the action line?

options.A: Discharge the patient home for two more days of rest
options.B: Stop all monitoring procedures until the second stage begins
options.C: Initiate active intervention such as augmentation or surgical review
options.D: Encourage the mother to walk around the ward corridors more

explanation: Crossing the action line warns that labour is prolonged or obstructed, requiring prompt medical evaluation and intervention. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h6)

question: Which complication is associated with the administration of systemic opioids like pethidine too close to the time of birth?

options.A: Severe maternal hypertension
options.B: Immediate postpartum hemorrhage
options.C: Prolonged third stage of labour
options.D: Neonatal respiratory depression

explanation: Opioids cross the placenta and can suppress the newborn's respiratory drive if given shortly before delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: What is a major advantage of utilizing continuous emotional support and back massage during labour?

options.A: They completely eliminate the need for cervical dilation checks
options.B: They accelerate the cardinal movements of the fetus automatically
options.C: They replace the requirement for partograph documentation
options.D: They offer non-pharmacological relief without systemic side effects for the baby

explanation: Non-pharmacological comfort measures help women cope with pain safely without introducing drugs that could affect the fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h7)

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely assessed in a newborn?

options.A: At birth and every hour thereafter
options.B: At 5 and 10 minutes after birth
options.C: At 10 and 30 minutes after birth
options.D: At 1 and 5 minutes after birth

explanation: The Apgar score is standardly evaluated at one minute to gauge immediate transition and at five minutes to assess response to resuscitation if needed. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of immediate skin-to-skin contact between mother and newborn following a normal delivery?

options.A: To eliminate the need for vitamin K administration
options.B: To measure the exact birth weight of the infant
options.C: To accelerate the delivery of the placenta
options.D: To promote thermal regulation and early bonding

explanation: Skin-to-skin contact utilizes maternal body heat to prevent hypothermia while fostering maternal-infant attachment and breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T002#GNS226_U3_T002_h8)

question: What gestational age range defines a term pregnancy for normal labour?

options.A: 34 to 38 completed weeks
options.B: 40 to 44 completed weeks
options.C: 37 to 42 completed weeks
options.D: 32 to 36 completed weeks

explanation: Normal labour typically occurs at term, which is clinically defined as a gestation lasting from 37 weeks up to the end of 42 weeks. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h1)

question: Which of the following represents the passenger in the context of labour dynamics?

options.A: Uterine contractions
options.B: The fetus
options.C: Maternal anxiety levels
options.D: The bony pelvis

explanation: The passenger refers to the fetus, whose size, presentation, and position greatly influence the mechanism of labour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h1)

question: What term is used to describe the positional adjustments a fetus makes while navigating the pelvis?

options.A: Uterine involution stages
options.B: Cardinal movements of labour
options.C: Placental separation phases
options.D: Pelvic floor relaxation drills

explanation: The series of physical adaptations the fetus makes through the birth canal are collectively called the cardinal movements. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h2)

question: Why does the fetus perform multiple positional changes during its transit through the pelvis?

options.A: To stimulate increased frequency of uterine contractions
options.B: To conserve fetal oxygen reserves during the second stage
options.C: To adapt its head diameters to the changing pelvic dimensions
options.D: To accelerate the detachment of the placenta from the wall

explanation: The bony pelvis changes shape from the inlet to the outlet, requiring the fetal head to rotate and flex to fit through the tightest spaces. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h2)

question: What anatomical landmark of the maternal pelvis signifies that engagement has occurred when reached by the biparietal diameter?

options.A: Sacral promontory
options.B: Pubic symphysis
options.C: Coccyx tip
options.D: Ischial spines

explanation: Engagement is confirmed when the widest part of the fetal head descends to the level of the ischial spines, corresponding to station zero. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h3)

question: When does engagement typically take place in a first-time mother (primigravida)?

options.A: A few weeks before the onset of labour
options.B: Immediately following the rupture of membranes
options.C: Only after the second stage of labour begins
options.D: During the third stage alongside the placenta

explanation: First-time mothers often experience head engagement late in the third trimester, weeks before actual labour contractions commence. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h3)

question: Which smaller fetal head diameter is achieved when optimal flexion occurs?

options.A: Suboccipito-bregmatic
options.B: Occipitofrontal
options.C: Submento-bregmatic
options.D: Mentovertical

explanation: Flexion tucks the chin to the chest, replacing the wider occipitofrontal diameter with the compact suboccipito-bregmatic diameter. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h4)

question: What anatomical structure of the pelvis is primarily responsible for triggering internal rotation of the fetal head?

options.A: Levator ani muscles
options.B: Obturator membrane
options.C: Sacral promontory
options.D: Inguinal ligament

explanation: The sloping pelvic floor muscles act like a slide, directing the leading occiput to rotate forward toward the pubic symphysis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h4)

question: Which maternal bone acts as a pivoting fulcrum during the extension of the fetal head?

options.A: Coccyx
options.B: Ischial tuberosity
options.C: Iliac crest
options.D: Pubic symphysis

explanation: The occiput pivots around the lower border of the pubic symphysis, allowing the face and chin to sweep upward and out. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h5)

question: What part of the fetus emerges first during the extension phase of a normal vertex delivery?

options.A: The vertex
options.B: The forehead
options.C: The occiput
options.D: The chin

explanation: As the head extends around the pubic bone, the vertex, brow, face, and chin successively sweep over the perineum and emerge. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h5)

question: What is the primary cause of restitution immediately following the birth of the head?

options.A: An intentional manual maneuver performed by the attending midwife
options.B: The sudden relaxation of the maternal perineal floor muscles
options.C: The untwisting of the neck vessels and tissues after internal rotation
options.D: The immediate contraction of the fetal shoulder girdle muscles

explanation: Restitution is a passive unwinding movement caused by the relief of torsion placed on the neck tissues during internal rotation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h6)

question: Which part of the fetal body is delivered immediately after the anterior shoulder during the expulsion phase?

options.A: The umbilical cord loop
options.B: The fetal buttocks
options.C: Both lower extremities
options.D: The posterior shoulder

explanation: The anterior shoulder delivers first under the pubic arch, after which the trunk flexes laterally to allow the posterior shoulder to sweep over the perineum. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T005#GNS226_U3_T005_h6)

question: What gestational age range defines a term pregnancy for normal labour?

options.A: 37 to 42 completed weeks
options.B: 34 to 38 completed weeks
options.C: 40 to 44 completed weeks
options.D: 28 to 36 completed weeks

explanation: A pregnancy is considered at term when it reaches between 37 and 42 completed weeks of gestation, which is the optimal window for a normal spontaneous delivery. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: Which clinical feature definitively distinguishes true labour from false labour?

options.A: Presence of mild lower abdominal discomfort
options.B: Progressive cervical dilation and effacement
options.C: Irregular tightening felt in the upper abdomen
options.D: Immediate relief of contractions with rest

explanation: True labour is fundamentally defined by progressive changes to the cervix, specifically effacement and dilation, alongside regular contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h1)

question: The second stage of labour officially concludes with which event?

options.A: Stabilization of maternal vital signs
options.B: Full dilation of the uterine cervix
options.C: Expulsion of the placenta and membranes
options.D: Complete delivery of the neonate

explanation: The second stage starts at full cervical dilation and ends precisely when the baby is completely born. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: What primary physiological mechanism prevents excessive bleeding during the third stage of labour?

options.A: Uterine muscle retraction and compression of blood vessels
options.B: Mechanical pressure from the resting maternal bladder
options.C: Vasoconstriction caused by endogenous oxytocin release
options.D: Clotting factor activation triggered by amniotic fluid

explanation: Living ligatures formed by interlacing uterine smooth muscle fibers contract and retract around open maternal vessels after placental separation, halting bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h2)

question: When is the optimal time to auscultate the fetal heart rate during the initial evaluation?

options.A: Only when membranes are confirmed ruptured
options.B: During active maternal pushing efforts
options.C: At the peak of a strong contraction
options.D: Immediately after a uterine contraction

explanation: Auscultating immediately after a contraction allows the midwife to detect fetal recovery and accurately assess baseline heart rate without missing decelerations caused by uterine compression. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: Why is sterile technique critical during the initial vaginal examination in labour?

options.A: To reduce the intensity of maternal contraction pain
options.B: To accelerate the rate of natural cervical dilation
options.C: To prevent premature rupture of the amniotic sac
options.D: To prevent ascending bacterial infection into the intrauterine cavity

explanation: Introducing unsterile fingers into the vagina increases the risk of microorganisms ascending into the uterus, potentially causing chorioamnionitis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h3)

question: How often should the fetal heart rate be checked during the active phase of the first stage of labour?

options.A: Every 2 hours
options.B: Every 5 minutes
options.C: Every 30 minutes
options.D: Once every hour

explanation: Current guidelines recommend auscultating the fetal heart rate at least every thirty minutes during the active first stage of labour to catch early signs of fetal distress. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: A labouring woman at 6 cm dilation reports an urge to void, but notes she has not passed urine for four hours. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?

options.A: Administer a rapid intravenous fluid bolus to stimulate renal clearance
options.B: Restrict all oral fluids to prevent bladder distension during contractions
options.C: Perform an immediate repeat vaginal examination to check cervical progress
options.D: Encourage her to attempt micturition, as a full bladder can obstruct fetal descent

explanation: A full bladder reduces uterine contractility and mechanically obstructs the descent of the presenting part, making bladder evacuation a priority. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h4)

question: Which maternal position is generally recommended during the second stage of labour to avoid aortocaval compression?

options.A: Upright or lateral position
options.B: High lithotomy position
options.C: Trendelenburg position
options.D: Flat supine position

explanation: An upright or lateral position prevents the heavy uterus from compressing the maternal aorta and inferior vena cava, maintaining optimal cardiac output and placental perfusion. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: What is the primary rationale for controlling the delivery of the fetal head as it crowns?

options.A: To delay birth until a physician is physically present at the bedside
options.B: To ensure the umbilical cord remains tightly wrapped around the neck
options.C: To prevent rapid expulsion that can cause severe perineal tearing
options.D: To artificially extend the duration of the second stage of labour

explanation: Controlled delivery allows gradual stretching of perineal tissues, significantly reducing the incidence of severe perineal lacerations. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h5)

question: What is the recommended uterotonic drug and standard dose for routine AMTSL?

options.A: Prostaglandin F2-alpha 250 micrograms
options.B: Misoprostol 800 micrograms orally
options.C: Oxytocin 10 International Units intramuscularly
options.D: Ergometrine 0.5 milligrams intravenously

explanation: Oxytocin 10 IU IM is the gold-standard uterotonic for AMTSL because it acts rapidly with minimal side effects compared to alternatives. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: Why must oxytocin be administered before attempting controlled cord traction during the third stage?

options.A: To induce uterine contraction and prevent uterine inversion
options.B: To accelerate the detachment of the fetal membranes
options.C: To prevent the umbilical cord from snapping prematurely
options.D: To numb maternal pelvic pain during placental expulsion

explanation: Giving oxytocin first ensures the uterus is contracted and firm, providing a safe anchor that prevents the organ from turning inside out during cord traction. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h6)

question: How often should maternal vital signs and uterine tone be assessed during the first hour of the fourth stage of labour?

options.A: Every 15 minutes
options.B: Every 30 minutes
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every hour

explanation: Because postpartum hemorrhage occurs most frequently in the immediate aftermath of delivery, vital signs and uterine tone are checked every 15 minutes during the first hour. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: What is the primary clinical implication of finding a boggy, soft uterus during immediate postpartum monitoring?

options.A: The placenta has not yet fully separated from the uterine wall
options.B: The infant has initiated effective suckling at the breast
options.C: The patient is experiencing uterine atony and is at risk for hemorrhage
options.D: The maternal bladder is completely empty and functioning normally

explanation: A soft or boggy uterus fails to clamp down on open maternal vessels, indicating uterine atony which can quickly lead to heavy postpartum bleeding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h7)

question: What clinical action is required when a labouring woman's partograph cervical dilation curve crosses to the right of the action line?

options.A: Immediate medical intervention or transfer for specialized management
options.B: Immediate cessation of all ongoing intravenous fluid therapy
options.C: Routine observation with no change in the current care plan
options.D: Discharge of the patient home for continued false labour monitoring

explanation: Crossing the action line indicates that labour is significantly delayed, requiring decisive intervention such as augmentation, operative delivery, or facility transfer. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)

question: What does the alert line on the World Health Organization partograph represent?

options.A: The exact moment when the second stage of labour begins
options.B: The threshold where fetal distress invariably occurs
options.C: The slowest expected rate of normal cervical dilation
options.D: The time limit for administering oxytocin augmentation

explanation: The alert line represents a dilation rate of 1 centimeter per hour, serving as a warning flag when labour progression drops below the normal curve. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T006#GNS226_U3_T006_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of a partograph during childbirth?

options.A: To provide a graphical overview of labour progress and maternal-fetal wellbeing
options.B: To serve as a legal birth certificate for the newborn infant
options.C: To calculate the exact financial cost of the maternity hospital admission
options.D: To record the complete immunization history of the mother

explanation: The partograph is specifically designed to track labour graphically so clinicians can monitor mother and baby simultaneously. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h1)

question: Why is the partograph considered an early warning system in busy clinical settings?

options.A: It alerts the hospital security team if delivery is delayed
options.B: It sounds an audible alarm whenever contractions become too strong
options.C: It turns complex observations into visual trends that highlight deviations early
options.D: It automatically administers oxytocin when labour slows down

explanation: Visual graphing makes it immediately obvious when labour parameters cross safety thresholds, prompting timely intervention. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h1)

question: Which of the following parameters is recorded in the fetal condition section of the partograph?

options.A: Volume of maternal urine output
options.B: Maternal blood pressure and temperature
options.C: Fetal heart rate and amniotic fluid color
options.D: Frequency of maternal uterine contractions

explanation: Fetal heart rate, liquor status, and molding directly assess the baby and belong in the fetal condition tier. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h2)

question: What is the clinical rationale for dividing the partograph into specific sections like progress, maternal status, and fetal condition?

options.A: It ensures that different nurses fill out different pages of the chart
options.B: It prevents doctors from reading the sections meant exclusively for midwives
options.C: It organizes diverse physiological data into a clear, easy-to-read visual format
options.D: It reduces the total number of vital signs that need to be measured

explanation: Segmenting the chart keeps complex labour data organized, allowing rapid multidisciplinary assessment at a glance. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h2)

question: What does a molding grade of +3 indicate on the partograph?

options.A: Complete crowning of the fetal head at the perineum
options.B: Normal separation of fetal skull sutures with wide fontanelles
options.C: Premature fusion of the cranial bones before the onset of labour
options.D: Severe overlapping of fetal skull bones that cannot be easily separated

explanation: Molding grade +3 signifies severe overlapping of the cranial bones, strongly suggesting cephalopelvic disproportion or obstruction. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h3)

question: A nurse notes thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid when membranes rupture. What does this finding primarily suggest?

options.A: Imminent placental detachment and normal delivery
options.B: Normal physiological progression of the first stage of labour
options.C: Potential fetal hypoxia or distress
options.D: Advanced maternal dehydration requiring oral fluids

explanation: The passage of meconium in cephalic presentation often indicates that the fetus has experienced hypoxic stress, prompting heightened surveillance. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h3)

question: How often is cervical dilatation routinely assessed and plotted during the active phase of normal labour?

options.A: Once every shift
options.B: Every 4 hours
options.C: Every 15 minutes
options.D: Every 2 hours

explanation: Standard partograph protocol dictates vaginal examinations every four hours to minimize infection risk while tracking cervical change. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h4)

question: A patient's cervical dilatation has remained at 5 cm for over four hours with adequate contractions. What does this indicate about her labour?

options.A: Normal progression along the alert line
options.B: Rapid descent typical of a multiparous precipitate delivery
options.C: Premature rupture of membranes without labour onset
options.D: Prolonged active phase requiring clinical review

explanation: A failure to dilate by at least 1 cm per hour in the active phase indicates slow progress, necessitating medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h4)

question: How frequently should maternal pulse be measured and recorded on the standard partograph?

options.A: Once every hour
options.B: Every 4 hours
options.C: Every 30 minutes
options.D: Every 2 hours

explanation: Maternal pulse is monitored half-hourly to catch early cardiovascular changes, dehydration, or impending shock. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h5)

question: What does the presence of acetone (ketones) in the maternal urine during labour signify?

options.A: A normal physiological reaction to epidural anesthesia
options.B: Bacterial urinary tract infection requiring antibiotics
options.C: Maternal starvation, dehydration, or prolonged energy depletion
options.D: Impending renal failure due to gestational hypertension

explanation: Ketones appear in urine when the body breaks down fat for energy due to inadequate caloric intake or dehydration during long labours. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h5)

question: At what cervical dilatation do the alert and action lines traditionally begin on the WHO partograph?

options.A: 10 cm
options.B: 4 cm
options.C: 7 cm
options.D: 0 cm

explanation: The active phase of labour is defined as starting at 4 cm dilatation, which is where the alert and action lines originate. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h6)

question: What clinical action is required when a parturient woman's cervical dilatation curve crosses the action line?

options.A: Routine observation for another four hours without changes
options.B: Immediate discontinuation of all intravenous fluid therapy
options.C: Discharge home for rest until contractions become stronger
options.D: Immediate medical evaluation and management intervention

explanation: Crossing the action line means labour is significantly prolonged, requiring active medical intervention to prevent complications. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h6)

question: What is the primary professional danger of retroactive or falsified charting on a partograph?

options.A: It automatically invalidates the nursing student's clinical logbook
options.B: It obscures true clinical deterioration and delays emergency interventions
options.C: It makes the paper chart difficult to photocopy for research
options.D: It violates administrative hospital dress code policies

explanation: Inaccurate or delayed charting masks the real-time condition of mother and baby, leading to missed warnings of distress. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct nursing responsibility when managing a patient in active labour with a partograph?

options.A: Performing spontaneous vacuum extractions without medical supervision
options.B: Monitoring and charting maternal vital signs consistently
options.C: Auscultating and recording fetal heart rate at regular intervals
options.D: Plotting cervical dilatation accurately during vaginal exams

explanation: Operative deliveries like vacuum extraction require advanced medical training and supervision, outside basic nursing scope. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T007#GNS226_U3_T007_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a clean birth kit in community obstetric care?

options.A: To eliminate the need for skilled birth attendants
options.B: To induce uterine contractions in preterm labor
options.C: To accelerate the progression of active labor
options.D: To minimize infection risks during childbirth

explanation: Clean birth kits provide sterile and hygienic components that interrupt contamination pathways leading to infections like neonatal tetanus and puerperal sepsis. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h1)

question: Why is a clean plastic sheet included as a fundamental component of a clean birth kit?

options.A: To collect blood loss for accurate postpartum hemorrhage estimation
options.B: To provide a dry, non-contaminated surface for the delivery
options.C: To serve as an improvised thermal wrap for the placenta
options.D: To protect the birth attendant's clothing from amniotic fluid

explanation: Laying a clean plastic sheet on the delivery surface prevents the mother and newborn from direct contact with contaminated ground or bedding. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h1)

question: What environmental factor is critical to prevent hypothermia in a newly delivered infant?

options.A: Continuous forced air ventilation
options.B: High humidity levels in the ward
options.C: A warm, draft-free delivery room
options.D: Bright overhead fluorescent lighting

explanation: Newborns lose heat rapidly through convection and evaporation; maintaining a warm and draft-free room protects them from dangerous drops in body temperature. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h2)

question: Why must emergency resuscitation equipment be checked and arranged prior to the second stage of labor?

options.A: To prevent the need for documenting intrapartum events later
options.B: To ensure immediate readiness if neonatal compromise occurs
options.C: To comply with administrative hospital accreditation checklists
options.D: To demonstrate advanced clinical competence to the laboring mother

explanation: Intrapartum complications can arise unexpectedly, and having functional resuscitation tools ready prevents critical delays in newborn intervention. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h2)

question: What is the primary clinical instrument used internationally to track the progress of labor?

options.A: The partograph
options.B: The pelvimetry grid
options.C: The Apgar chart
options.D: The Bishop score

explanation: The partograph is a pictorial overview of labor that helps detect deviations from normal progress for both mother and fetus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h3)

question: Which assessment finding during labor demands immediate evaluation for fetal distress?

options.A: Spontaneous rupture of membranes with clear amniotic fluid
options.B: Regular uterine contractions occurring every three minutes
options.C: Maternal blood pressure reading of 120/80 millimeters of mercury
options.D: Fetal heart rate dropping below 110 beats per minute

explanation: A baseline fetal heart rate below 110 beats per minute or above 160 beats per minute suggests potential hypoxia and requires urgent investigation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the essential cleans recommended during safe delivery?

options.A: Clean intravenous access
options.B: Clean hands and fingernails
options.C: Clean cord management
options.D: Clean delivery surface

explanation: Routine intravenous access is not listed among the essential cleans, which focus on hand hygiene, clean surfaces, perineal care, and sterile cord handling. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h4)

question: What infection is primarily prevented by practicing strict hygiene during umbilical cord cutting and tying?

options.A: Respiratory distress syndrome
options.B: Neonatal jaundice
options.C: Neonatal tetanus
options.D: Congenital syphilis

explanation: Using unsterile instruments or tying the cord with contaminated materials introduces Clostridium tetani spores, resulting in fatal neonatal tetanus. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h4)

question: At what specific time intervals is the Apgar score routinely assessed after birth?

options.A: Ten and twenty minutes
options.B: Immediately and thirty minutes
options.C: One and five minutes
options.D: Five and ten minutes

explanation: Standard neonatal assessment protocols require Apgar scoring at one minute to evaluate immediate tolerance to birth and at five minutes to gauge response to resuscitation or extrauterine adaptation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of initiating immediate skin-to-skin contact between mother and newborn?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for subsequent vitamin K administration
options.B: It stabilizes infant temperature and encourages early breastfeeding
options.C: It accelerates the natural detachment of the umbilical cord stump
options.D: It guarantees an Apgar score of ten out of ten within minutes

explanation: Skin-to-skin contact harnesses maternal body heat to prevent hypothermia and stimulates instinctive feeding behaviors in the infant. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h5)

question: What is the preferred uterotonic drug administered during the active management of the third stage of labor?

options.A: Nifedipine
options.B: Oxytocin
options.C: Hydralazine
options.D: Magnesium sulfate

explanation: Oxytocin is recommended because it effectively contracts the myometrium with a fast onset and fewer adverse systemic effects than alternative agents. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h6)

question: What is the primary clinical objective of performing controlled cord traction alongside uterine counter-pressure?

options.A: To stimulate milk letdown prior to infant suckling
options.B: To measure the exact volume of residual amniotic fluid
options.C: To force the closure of the maternal cervical os
options.D: To facilitate safe and timely delivery of the placenta

explanation: Controlled cord traction combined with suprapubic counter-pressure safely guides the placenta out of the uterus while preventing uterine inversion. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h6)

question: What is considered the single most effective measure to prevent hospital-acquired infections in maternity wards?

options.A: Routine prophylactic antibiotic therapy
options.B: Wearing sterile gowns for all examinations
options.C: Frequent and proper hand hygiene
options.D: Daily changing of room air filters

explanation: Handwashing with soap and water or alcohol-based hand rub removes transient flora and stops the transmission of pathogens between patients. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h7)

question: Why must used injection needles and surgical blades never be recapped after assisting with a delivery?

options.A: To comply with waste management laws regarding chemical disposal
options.B: To prevent accidental needlestick injuries to the healthcare worker
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing safety-engineered devices
options.D: To ensure instruments are immediately available for the next patient

explanation: Recapping needles is a primary cause of accidental sharps injuries, which expose personnel to blood-borne pathogens like hepatitis and HIV. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h7)

question: What is the drug of choice for managing eclamptic seizures during labor and delivery?

options.A: Diazepam
options.B: Calcium gluconate
options.C: Magnesium sulfate
options.D: Phenytoin

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the internationally established anticonvulsant used to control and prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h8)

question: What immediate physical maneuver is indicated when a patient experiences shoulder dystocia during delivery?

options.A: Flexing the mother's thighs tightly against her abdomen
options.B: Performing an immediate elective forceps extraction
options.C: Placing the mother in a prone position on the delivery bed
options.D: Applying heavy downward fundal pressure to push the baby

explanation: The McRoberts maneuver involves hyperflexing the maternal legs, which flattens the sacrum and rotates the symphysis pubis upward to release the impacted shoulder. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h8)

question: How often should maternal vital signs and uterine tone be monitored during the immediate two-hour postpartum period?

options.A: Every hour for the first four hours without interruption
options.B: Every fifteen minutes for the first hour, then every thirty minutes
options.C: Only when the patient complains of dizziness or pain
options.D: Once every shift before nursing handover takes place

explanation: Frequent initial monitoring catches early signs of postpartum hemorrhage and hemodynamic instability when intervention is most effective. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h9)

question: Why is contemporaneous nursing documentation of delivery events critically important?

options.A: It provides an accurate legal record and ensures safe shift handover
options.B: It prevents the mother from experiencing postpartum depression
options.C: It automatically calculates the hospital billing for obstetric services
options.D: It eliminates the need for verbal communication between clinicians

explanation: Contemporaneous documentation prevents memory lapses, guides ongoing clinical care, and stands as a legal defense for professional actions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T008#GNS226_U3_T008_h9)

question: What is the primary objective of Essential Obstetric Care?

options.A: To guarantee home deliveries for low-risk pregnancies
options.B: To eliminate the need for physician intervention during birth
options.C: To reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality
options.D: To provide routine antenatal vitamins to all pregnant women

explanation: The overarching goal of this framework is saving lives by addressing life-threatening complications during pregnancy and childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h1)

question: Why is the categorization of obstetric care into basic and comprehensive levels important?

options.A: It differentiates normal physiological labor from complicated surgical births
options.B: It restricts advanced medical procedures exclusively to university teaching hospitals
options.C: It ensures appropriate resource allocation and timely patient routing
options.D: It dictates the exact salary scale for attending midwives and nurses

explanation: Categorizing care levels helps health systems match facility capabilities with clinical needs, preventing avoidable delays. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h1)

question: How many signal functions define Basic Emergency Obstetric Care (BEmOC)?

options.A: Twelve signal functions
options.B: Nine signal functions
options.C: Five signal functions
options.D: Seven signal functions

explanation: BEmOC is internationally defined by a specific set of seven clinical interventions that lower maternal and neonatal mortality at the primary care level. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h2)

question: A primigravida at a primary health centre develops severe pre-eclampsia with hyperreflexia. Which BEmOC signal function must the nurse administer immediately?

options.A: Assisted vaginal delivery
options.B: Manual removal of placenta
options.C: Parenteral anticonvulsants
options.D: Parenteral antibiotics

explanation: Magnesium sulfate is the standard parenteral anticonvulsant required under BEmOC signal functions to manage eclamptic seizures. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h2)

question: Which two additional capabilities distinguish Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care (CEmOC) from BEmOC?

options.A: Manual vacuum aspiration and parenteral antibiotic therapy
options.B: Cesarean section delivery and blood transfusion services
options.C: Antenatal ultrasound scanning and routine genetic counseling
options.D: Specialized neonatal intensive care and mechanical ventilation

explanation: CEmOC facilities add surgical capacity and blood banking to the seven basic signal functions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h3)

question: A multiparous woman presents with complete uterine rupture. What level of obstetric facility is mandatory for her definitive surgical management?

options.A: Basic Emergency Obstetric Care clinic
options.B: Traditional birth attendant homestead
options.C: Comprehensive Emergency Obstetric Care facility
options.D: Primary health care post without maternity beds

explanation: Uterine rupture requires immediate exploratory laparotomy and blood transfusion, which are exclusive to CEmOC facilities. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h3)

question: What is the primary physical sign indicating impending or actual uterine rupture during obstructed labor?

options.A: Immediate spontaneous rupture of amniotic membranes
options.B: Continuous painless contractions of the myometrium
options.C: Formation of a pathological retraction ring
options.D: Rapid descent of the fetal head into the pelvis

explanation: Bandl's ring represents the extreme thinning and stretching of the lower uterine segment, signaling imminent rupture. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h4)

question: A postpartum woman saturates two perineal pads within fifteen minutes and exhibits a boggy uterus. What is the priority nursing action?

options.A: Perform immediate bimanual uterine massage
options.B: Encourage early ambulation to stimulate uterine tone
options.C: Collect blood samples for routine hematocrit analysis
options.D: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for baseline output

explanation: A boggy uterus indicates uterine atony; immediate massage stimulates contraction to occlude open maternal blood vessels. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h4)

question: Why is left uterine displacement performed during maternal cardiac arrest or collapse past twenty weeks of gestation?

options.A: To encourage spontaneous descent of the fetal presenting part
options.B: To facilitate rapid emergency cesarean section at the bedside
options.C: To prevent the umbilical cord from prolapsing into the vagina
options.D: To relieve aortocaval compression and improve cardiac output

explanation: The heavy gravid uterus compresses the aorta and inferior vena cava when a woman lies flat, severely dropping cardiac output. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h5)

question: Which intervention takes precedence when resuscitating a woman experiencing severe hemorrhagic shock?

options.A: Performing a complete neurological reflex examination
options.B: Securing large-bore intravenous access for volume replacement
options.C: Obtaining a detailed family history of bleeding disorders
options.D: Administering broad-spectrum prophylactic oral antibiotics

explanation: Restoring intravascular volume is the immediate priority to reverse shock and maintain vital organ perfusion. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h5)

question: How often should the fetal heart rate be auscultated and recorded on the partograph during the active phase of labor?

options.A: Every 30 minutes
options.B: Once every shift
options.C: Every 4 hours
options.D: Every 2 hours

explanation: Frequent auscultation of the fetal heart rate is necessary to catch early signs of fetal distress during active contractions. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h6)

question: What clinical decision is indicated when a laboring woman's cervical dilatation curve crosses the action line on the partograph?

options.A: Discharge home because labor has temporarily arrested
options.B: Immediate discontinuation of all oxytocin infusions and hydration
options.C: Immediate evaluation for intervention or expedited delivery
options.D: Continuation of routine expectant monitoring for another four hours

explanation: The action line signifies that active management or surgical delivery is required to prevent severe maternal and fetal morbidity. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of decontaminating and sterilizing surgical instruments used in the labor ward?

options.A: To extend the physical lifespan of stainless steel instruments
options.B: To remove chemical residues from previous pharmaceutical batches
options.C: To break the chain of transmission for healthcare-associated pathogens
options.D: To comply with administrative hospital accreditation requirements

explanation: Sterilization destroys all microbial life, preventing the introduction of pathogens into the reproductive tract during childbirth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h7)

question: Which infection control practice is NOT recommended during routine vaginal examinations in labor?

options.A: Performing thorough hand hygiene before donning protective barriers
options.B: Segregating sharp needles immediately into puncture-resistant safety boxes
options.C: Reusing single-use disposable sterile gloves after washing them with soap
options.D: Wearing water-resistant aprons to protect against amniotic fluid splashes

explanation: Disposable gloves are single-use items; washing and reusing them compromises their structural integrity and sterility. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h7)

question: Which delay in the three-delays model is primarily addressed by establishing effective emergency transport and referral networks?

options.A: Delay in receiving treatment after arrival
options.B: Delay in recognizing symptoms at home
options.C: Delay in deciding to seek care
options.D: Delay in reaching a medical facility

explanation: Transport and referral systems specifically target the geographic and logistical barriers encountered when traveling to care. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h8)

question: What action should the nurse-midwife take prior to dispatching a complicated obstetric patient via emergency transport?

options.A: Wait for family members to settle all hospital financial balances
options.B: Stabilize the patient's vital signs and send the partograph records
options.C: Await complete natural delivery of the infant at the primary clinic
options.D: Discontinue all intravenous infusions to prevent needle dislodgement

explanation: Stabilization and accompanying clinical documentation ensure continuity of care and safe transit for the patient. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T009#GNS226_U3_T009_h8)

question: What primary physiological change occurs in the pulmonary vasculature immediately after successful newborn air breathing?

options.A: Pulmonary vascular resistance decreases significantly
options.B: Pulmonary blood flow ceases entirely
options.C: Pulmonary vascular resistance increases sharply
options.D: Pulmonary arterial pressure remains identical to fetal levels

explanation: Air entry into the alveoli causes the pulmonary blood vessels to relax, which drastically lowers resistance and allows blood to flood the lungs for oxygenation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h1)

question: Why does clamping of the umbilical cord contribute to systemic blood pressure elevation in the neonate?

options.A: It removes the low-resistance placental vascular bed
options.B: It directly stimulates the left ventricle to pump faster
options.C: It causes immediate constriction of the aorta
options.D: It forces residual blood from the cord into the right atrium

explanation: The placenta acts as a large low-resistance circuit; once severed, systemic vascular resistance rises, which helps push blood through the newly opened lung pathways. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h1)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the initial three rapid assessment questions asked immediately at a newborn's birth?

options.A: Is the baby breathing or crying?
options.B: Is the baby term or preterm?
options.C: Is the amniotic fluid clear?
options.D: Is the newborn passing meconium stool?

explanation: Passing stool is not evaluated in the first seconds of life; the team focuses strictly on gestation, liquor clarity, and breathing or crying effort. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h2)

question: What is the primary clinical significance of meconium-stained amniotic fluid during delivery preparation?

options.A: It proves the mother has gestational diabetes
options.B: It confirms the exact gestational age of the fetus
options.C: It indicates an uncomplicated and rapid second stage of labor
options.D: It signals potential fetal compromise and the risk of airway obstruction

explanation: Meconium passage in utero often reflects fetal distress, and aspiration of stained fluid into the lungs can cause severe respiratory complications after birth. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h2)

question: What is the main purpose of drying a newborn immediately after birth?

options.A: To stimulate the central nervous system into producing surfactant
options.B: To remove all vernix caseosa permanently from the skin
options.C: To increase systemic blood pressure instantly
options.D: To prevent evaporative heat loss and hypothermia

explanation: Wet skin rapidly loses heat through evaporation in the delivery room environment, making prompt drying essential to maintaining normal body temperature. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h3)

question: Why is delayed cord clamping generally recommended for vigorous term newborns?

options.A: It guarantees the infant will never develop jaundice
options.B: It eliminates the need for any subsequent physical examinations
options.C: It enhances placental transfusion, improving neonatal iron stores
options.D: It prevents the closure of the ductus arteriosus

explanation: Allowing blood to continue flowing from the placenta for a short period provides extra red blood cells, which protects against iron deficiency anemia in early infancy. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h3)

question: In what order should the newborn airway be suctioned when heavy secretions are present?

options.A: Mouth first, then the nose
options.B: Nose first, then the mouth
options.C: The trachea directly using a deep catheter
options.D: Both nostrils simultaneously before the mouth

explanation: Suctioning the mouth first prevents the infant from gasping and aspirating pooled oral secretions when the nasal passages are stimulated. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h4)

question: A newborn fails to breathe spontaneously after thorough drying and positioning. What is the safest and most appropriate next step?

options.A: Perform immediate chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
options.B: Slap the infant's buttocks firmly until a loud cry is produced
options.C: Administer emergency intravenous adrenaline immediately
options.D: Apply gentle tactile stimulation to the back or soles of the feet

explanation: Mild tactile stimulation is a safe, effective method to trigger a respiratory drive in secondary apnea before escalating to invasive ventilation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h4)

question: What is the recommended ventilation rate per minute when administering PPV to a newborn?

options.A: 120 to 140 breaths
options.B: 10 to 20 breaths
options.C: 80 to 100 breaths
options.D: 40 to 60 breaths

explanation: Maintaining a ventilation rate between 40 and 60 breaths per minute closely mimics normal neonatal respiratory rates during resuscitation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h5)

question: Why is the pulse oximeter sensor placed on the right wrist or hand during neonatal resuscitation?

options.A: It prevents the infant from dislodging the sensor with leg movements
options.B: It measures pre-ductal oxygen saturation before blood mixes with ductal shunts
options.C: It directly records electrical activity from the sinoatrial node
options.D: It is the only anatomical site with adequate skin perfusion in a newborn

explanation: The right arm receives blood directly from the brachiocephalic artery before it passes through the ductus arteriosus, reflecting true brain and heart oxygenation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h5)

question: What is the correct compression-to-ventilation ratio during neonatal resuscitation?

options.A: 30 compressions to 2 breaths
options.B: 5 compressions to 1 breath
options.C: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
options.D: 3 compressions to 1 breath

explanation: Neonatal arrest is primarily respiratory in origin, so resuscitation protocols use a 3:1 ratio to prioritize frequent ventilation alongside circulation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h6)

question: When should chest compressions be initiated for a compromised newborn?

options.A: Whenever the infant shows central cyanosis with a normal heart rate
options.B: When the heart rate is below 60 bpm after effective PPV for 30 seconds
options.C: As soon as the umbilical cord is clamped and cut
options.D: Immediately upon noting meconium-stained amniotic fluid at delivery

explanation: Compressions are reserved for severe bradycardia that does not improve despite ensuring adequate lung inflation through positive pressure ventilation. [learn more](GNS226_U3_T010#GNS226_U3_T010_h6)

question: What is the primary emergency medication used during neonatal resuscitation when bradycardia persists?

options.A: Atropine sulfate
options.B: Adrenaline (epinephrine)
options.C: Sodium bicarbonate
options.D: Calcium gluconate
